docs.title: Secrets Bridge
docs.text:
The agent runs inside your infrastructure and only calls out, so you open no inbound port.

  • No plaintext values in the control plane. Not in Postgres, Redis, logs, audit events or the browser. In transit, values are KMS-wrapped.
  • The agent only calls out. No inbound port, no database, no Kubernetes API access to Secrets.
  • Production never allows direct reveal. The refusal is enforced in code and audited.
  • Values move once. KMS-wrapped, single-use, short-lived, and opened only by the right person.
  • Audit is append-only and metadata-only. Who, what, when and why, never the value.
  • Agents are bound and revocable. One-time enrollment tokens, one provider connection per agent, revoked at once.

docs.title: Govern who uses your secrets.
docs.text:
Secrets Bridge adds access requests, approvals, audit and agent execution around the secrets you already keep in AWS Secrets Manager and HashiCorp Vault. We keep requests, approvals and audit metadata. Your secret values stay in your provider.

Run it locally Read the architecture Source on GitHub

Open source and pre-1.0. See what is live today and what is still on the roadmap.

docs.title: We keep
docs.text:
• Requests, and who approved them
  • The audit trail: who, what, when and why
  • Which secret paths and key names a project may use

docs.title: We never keep
docs.text:
• Secret values in plain text. In transit a value exists only as an encrypted, single-use wrap with a short lifetime.
  • Provider credentials. The agent uses its own, inside your infrastructure.

docs.title: Where your secrets go, and where they don't
docs.text:
Values stay in your provider until an approved request needs them. Then they travel once, sealed, and only to the person who asked. Pick a step to follow it.

Follow a request All steps Step 1: Ask for access Step 2: Someone approves Step 3: The agent claims the job Step 4: It reads the provider Step 5: It sends back a sealed wrap Step 6: Reveal once PEOPLE Requester asks, then reveals Approver decides SECRETS BRIDGE CONTROL PLANE Console and API sign-in, policy, second factor Requests, approvals, audit metadata only; audit is append-only Jobs and single-use wraps values sealed, opened once No plaintext values are kept here. YOUR INFRASTRUCTURE Agent calls out only no inbound port its own credentials PROVIDERS AWS Secrets Manager HashiCorp Vault KV v2 Values leave only as a sealed wrap. 1 6 2 3 5 4 opens the connection comes backProviders are reached only by the agent, inside your infrastructure. PEOPLE Requester asks, then reveals Approver decides CONTROL PLANE Console and API sign-in, policy, second factor Requests, approvals, audit metadata only; append-only audit Jobs and single-use wraps values sealed, opened once No plaintext values are kept here. YOUR INFRASTRUCTURE Agent calls out only; no inbound port AWS Secrets Manager HashiCorp Vault KV v2 1 6 2 3 5 4
  1. 1Ask for access. The requester names the secret, the keys and why. No value is sent.
  2. 2Someone approves. The policy for the project and environment decides how many approvals it needs and from whom.
  3. 3The agent claims the job. The agent calls out to the control plane for work. Nothing calls in, so you open no inbound port.
  4. 4It reads the provider. The agent reads only the approved keys, with its own credentials, inside your infrastructure.
  5. 5It sends back a sealed wrap. The values travel back encrypted for this request and are held only as a single-use wrap with a short lifetime.
  6. 6Reveal once. The requester confirms with a second factor and sees each value once. Every step is in the audit log.

docs.title: What it holds to
docs.text: These are enforced in code, not left to policy. The threat model shows how each boundary is kept.

docs.title: What works today
docs.text: Full product status, with what is QA-certified and what is in progress.

docs.title: Implemented
docs.text:
• AWS Secrets Manager and HashiCorp Vault through the agent
  • Read requests with policy-driven approval
  • Direct reveal in non-production, behind a second factor
  • Cross-team requests: another team supplies the values
  • Agent enrollment, status and revoke
  • Append-only audit trail

docs.text:

  • Deeper Kubernetes External Secrets integration
  • Flux integration

Not shipped. Don't plan around these yet.

docs.title: Start on your laptop
docs.text:
The api repo's compose file starts Postgres, Redis and the control plane; the console and the agent run from their own repos. The local guide walks through the whole flow against a dev Vault.

Run it locally Operations guide

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The project is split into nine repositories under the secrets-bridge GitHub organisation. Each one has a single responsibility; the dependency direction is one-way and reviewable.

Repo Language Holds core Go Provider interface + connectors, shared types. Infra-free: no Postgres, no Redis. api Go (Fiber v3) Control Plane API. Owns Postgres + Redis + the workflow/RBAC domain. worker Go Background sweepers, the GitOps observation poller, periodic discovery scheduler. agent Go Outbound-only execution agent. No Postgres / Redis dependency. controller Go (kubebuilder) Kubernetes CRD reconciler. Receives the v0.1.0 operator. gateway Go Optional, outbound-only, read-only observation of Argo CD rollout state. No Postgres / Redis, no Kubernetes client in Release 1. Release 1 in progress. ui React + TS + Vite SPA dashboard. No SSR. charts Helm / YAML Helm charts for the control plane, the agent and the Gateway (production deployment). docs mkdocs-material This site.

docs.title: Dependency graph
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    core["core<br/>provider interface +<br/>shared types"]
    api["api<br/>Postgres + Redis<br/>workflow + audit"]
    worker["worker<br/>sweepers + gitops"]
    agent["agent<br/>outbound only"]
    controller["controller<br/>K8s reconciler"]
    gateway["gateway<br/>outbound only,<br/>read-only"]
    ui["ui<br/>React SPA"]
    charts["charts<br/>Helm bundle"]

    api -->|"imports"| core
    worker -->|"imports"| api
    worker -->|"imports via pkg"| core
    agent -->|"imports"| core
    agent -.->|"HTTPS only"| api
    controller -->|"imports"| core
    ui -.->|"HTTPS only"| api
    gateway -.->|"HTTPS only"| api
    charts -.->|"deploys"| api
    charts -.->|"deploys"| worker
    charts -.->|"deploys"| agent
    charts -.->|"deploys"| controller
    charts -.->|"deploys"| ui
    charts -.->|"deploys"| gateway

The forbidden edges:

  • agent → api/internal/storage (would pull Postgres into the workload network)
  • agent → api/internal/runtime (would pull Redis)
  • controller → api/pkg/storage (same reasoning)
  • core → anything that imports database/sql / redis/*
  • gateway → api, worker, agent, controller, any database, Redis or KV driver, or k8s.io/client-go

CI in each repo greps go.sum to enforce these directions; the build fails if a forbidden module path appears.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
Repo: secrets-bridge/agent · Stack: Go 1.25 stdlib net/http (no Fiber) + hashicorp/vault/api + aws-sdk-go-v2/service/secretsmanager · Container: golang:1.25-alpine → distroless/static:nonroot

The execution tier. Runs inside the target account / cluster. Holds provider credentials for its own boundary only; the Control Plane never sees them.

docs.title: Hard rules enforced by CI
docs.text: Rule How No database driver CI greps go.sum for pgx, lib/pq, mysql, mongo-driver; fails on hit No Redis client CI greps go.sum for redis/go-redis, gomodule/redigo; fails on hit No inbound listener except probes The only listener serves /healthz, /readyz and /metrics on SB_LOCAL_ADDR. The binary defaults to 127.0.0.1:8090. The agent Helm chart binds 0.0.0.0:8090 because kubelet probes come from the node, creates no Service for it, and its default NetworkPolicy denies all ingress to the pod. Identity file mode 0600 TestSaveToFile_AtomicNoPartialOnFailure asserts the perm bits TLS required to the CP validateEndpoint refuses http:// unless SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true Plaintext zeroed after one use client.Zero([]byte) is called via defer on every value-bearing slice

docs.title: Boot sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Env
    participant Agent
    participant CP
    Agent->>Agent: validateEndpoint (https or fail)
    Agent->>Agent: load X25519 keypair<br/>(env / file / ephemeral)
    Env->>Agent: stored identity?<br/>(SB_IDENTITY_FILE, or SB_AGENT_ID + SB_AGENT_SECRET)
    alt no stored identity
        Env->>Agent: SB_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN (one-time)
        Agent->>CP: POST /agents/enroll
        CP-->>Agent: agent_id + agent_token (returned once)
        Agent->>Agent: write identity to SB_IDENTITY_FILE (0600)
    end
    Agent->>CP: PUT /agents/:id/public-key<br/>(register wire-envelope pubkey)
    CP-->>Agent: 204
    par Heartbeat loop
        loop every SB_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL
            Agent->>CP: POST /agents/:id/heartbeat
        end
    and Claim loop
        loop every SB_CLAIM_INTERVAL
            Agent->>CP: POST /agents/:id/jobs/claim
            CP-->>Agent: job or 204
        end
    end

Heartbeat response shape

A bodyless heartbeat returns an empty 204, the shape existing agents rely on. A heartbeat with an optional JSON body (status / agent_version / capabilities) returns 200 {status, server_time, next_heartbeat_seconds} and records the reported fields; the first heartbeat also transitions an enrolled agent to active. Agents are onboarded via the enrollment-token flow (POST /provider-connections/:id/agent-enrollment-token → POST /agents/enroll); see the HTTP API reference.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Env var Required Default Notes SB_CP_ENDPOINT yes - https://api.secrets-bridge.example SB_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN first boot - One-time token from POST /provider-connections/:id/agent-enrollment-token; spent once at POST /agents/enroll SB_ENROLLMENT_ENABLED no true Enroll on first boot when no identity is stored and a token is set SB_IDENTITY_FILE no /etc/secrets-bridge/identity.json Written after enrollment, read on every restart; must be writable and persistent SB_PROVIDER_TYPE no aws-sm Reported at enrollment; must match the provider connection's type SB_CLUSTER_NAME yes for discovery jobs - Stamped on every discovered secret SB_AGENT_ID / SB_AGENT_SECRET no - Pre-provisioned credential; overrides the identity file and skips enrollment SB_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL no 30s Bounded by api's stale-after window SB_CLAIM_INTERVAL no 5s Claim cadence SB_CLAIM_CONCURRENCY no 4 Worker pool size; non-blocking semaphore SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT no false Dev only: allows http:// to the CP (insecure switches) SB_CP_CA_FILE no - Pin a private CA (replaces system roots) SB_AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE no ephemeral X25519 keypair persistence Provider creds (per resolver) yes - See Providers supported

The full list, including SB_AGENT_NAME, SB_REGION and the provider settings, is in the configuration reference.

Direct mint is a dev-only break-glass

SB_AGENT_ID / SB_AGENT_SECRET only come from the legacy direct mint (POST /api/v1/agents), which the api refuses with 403 direct_agent_mint_disabled unless SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT=true. Onboard agents with an enrollment token instead; see Agent onboarding.

docs.title: Executors that ship today
docs.text: Job type Executor What it does patch PatchExecutor Fetches wraps → GetValue (existing bundle) → merge → PutValue → mark consumed. Idempotent re-runs (untouched keys survive). read ReadExecutor Fetches one bundle → selective target_keys split → POST /agents/:id/wraps per key → zero plaintext after each post discover DiscoverExecutor ListMetadata(scope) → preserve native tags verbatim into the CP's labels jsonb (Vault custom_metadata, AWS Tags, etc.)

docs.title: Provider resolvers
docs.text:
The agent dispatches by payload.target_provider_type via ResolverByType. Today:

Type Status Auth vault ✅ ships Token (SB_VAULT_TOKEN) or Kubernetes (SB_VAULT_KUBERNETES_ROLE) aws-sm ✅ ships Standard AWS SDK chain (IRSA / instance role / AWS_* env) gcp-sm placeholder Stub returns NotConfiguredResolver azure-kv placeholder Stub returns NotConfiguredResolver

Every resolver refuses credential-shaped keys in the target_provider_config (e.g. awsSecretAccessKey, token, sessionToken) so a future api bug can't accidentally ship a credential to the agent over the wire.

docs.title: Control Plane API (api)
docs.text:
Repo: secrets-bridge/api · Stack: Go 1.25 + Fiber v3 + pgx v5 + go-redis v9 · Container: golang:1.25-alpine build → distroless/static:nonroot

The decision-making tier. Holds metadata, owns the workflow + RBAC domain, mediates between users (via the SPA) and agents (via outbound HTTPS).

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
api/
├── cmd/api/                # main, config, server bootstrap
├── internal/
│   ├── auth/               # permission catalog, scope resolvers, auth.Require
│   ├── handlers/           # HTTP layer (one file per aggregate)
│   ├── middleware/         # Auth (session cookie), default-deny gate, RequestID, Logger, Recover
│   ├── observability/      # slog JSON logger
│   └── services/           # business logic (one file per aggregate)
└── pkg/
    ├── storage/            # Postgres repositories + migrations (embed.FS)
    ├── runtime/            # Redis primitives (locks, idempotency, rate limit, pub/sub)
    ├── keymgmt/            # KMS backends (local / vault-transit / aws-kms)
    ├── sealing/            # X25519 + HKDF + AES-GCM for wire envelope
    └── argocd/             # read-only ArgoCD client (BRD §26)

The internal/ boundary is closed; the pkg/ boundary is deliberately open because worker imports pkg/storage and pkg/keymgmt.

docs.title: How a request gets its identity
docs.text:
middleware.AuthWith resolves the caller once per request, in this order:

  1. Session cookie (sb_session, HttpOnly), issued by /auth/login and the sign-in callbacks. It is the only user credential: logout, session revocation and disabling the user end it.
  2. Otherwise the caller is anonymous, and the default-deny gate on /api/v1 answers 401 for every route that isn't explicitly public. Per-route auth.Require(perm) checks then run on top for authenticated callers.

Authorization: Bearer is not read for users. Login returns no token, so scripts keep the session cookie in a cookie jar (curl -c jar to sign in, -b jar after).

Agent routes under /api/v1/agents/:id/ authenticate separately, with the agent's X-Agent-Secret. POST /api/v1/agents/enroll authenticates with the one-time enrollment token in the body.

The legacy X-User-Id header is ignored unless the api runs with SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_HEADER_AUTH=true, a dev-only switch that lets anyone claim any identity. It is checked only after the session cookie, and it must never be set on a deployment anyone else can reach. See Insecure switches.

docs.title: Runtime endpoints
docs.text:
Path Purpose GET /healthz Always 200. Liveness. GET /readyz Aggregated readiness across postgres + redis checks (+ KMS at boot). 503 with per-check failure map on failure. GET /metrics Prometheus exposition. POST /api/v1/auth/login Email + password. Sets the sb_session cookie and returns {expires_at, user}.

See HTTP API endpoints for the full surface.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Env var Required Default Notes API_ADDR no :8080 Listen address DATABASE_URL yes - postgres://... REDIS_URL yes - redis://... SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY yes when SB_KMS_BACKEND=local - base64 32 bytes SB_KMS_BACKEND no local local / vault-transit / aws-kms SB_KMS_VAULT_ADDR / SB_KMS_VAULT_TOKEN / SB_KMS_VAULT_KEY yes for vault-transit - SB_KMS_AWS_REGION / SB_KMS_AWS_KEY_ID yes for aws-kms - Alias OK; ARN stored in audit SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL / SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD recommended on first boot - Seeds local-admin user; idempotent SB_GITOPS_ENABLED no false Mounts BRD §26 ArgoCD endpoints when true

See Configuration reference for the exhaustive list, including the dev-only insecure switches.

docs.title: What's stable, what isn't
docs.text: Area Status The four request lifecycles (submit / approve / reject / cancel) Stable Patch + read flows end-to-end against Vault + AWS SM Stable Single-shot wrap consumption Stable, race-tested (6 concurrent racers) Session-cookie login + auth.Require(perm) gating on write endpoints Stable OIDC sign-in (PKCE, group-to-role mapping, back-channel logout) Shipped; see Authentication Per-tenant KMS scoping Not shipped, tracked as Piece 8c Login brute-force defence Shipped: per-account lockout (5 wrong passwords, 15 minutes) plus per-IP rate limits on the auth routes and a per-agent heartbeat limit; see Authentication Tested key-rotation runbook Not shipped, tracked at api#31

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
Repo: secrets-bridge/controller · Stack: Go 1.26 + controller-runtime · Container: golang:1.26-alpine → distroless/static:nonroot

The Kubernetes operator. Receives the v0.1.0 CRD reconciler and is the GitOps consumer for cluster-internal sync.

docs.title: What ships
docs.text:
• api/v1alpha1 group with the SecretsSync CRD (ported verbatim from v0.1.0; only the module-path import changed)
  • The reconciler validates the CR by calling Providers.Build() for both refs and reports Ready=Validated / Ready=ProviderError. It does not run the sync loop itself
  • Provider registry injected on the Reconciler struct (matches the Register(r) pattern in core/providers/*)

docs.title: Key behavioural change from v0.1.0
docs.text:
The v0.1.0 reconciler embedded the sync engine. The new architecture moves execution to the agent (BRD §12.4):

What the new reconciler does What it deliberately doesn't Loads the CR Run a for name in source loop Validates refs via Providers.Build() Skip-if-unchanged content-hash comparison Sets Ready=Validated on success Read GetValue from any provider Sets Ready=ProviderError with the factory's text Write PutValue to any provider Re-queues every spec.refreshInterval Delete orphans

The sync work is dispatched to the agent via the CP's job queue. The controller is a GitOps gate for the cluster, not the executor.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Env var Required Default Notes KUBECONFIG for out-of-cluster runs - In-cluster uses the projected SA token LEADER_ELECTION_NAMESPACE no the controller's own namespace METRICS_ADDR no :8080 Prometheus exposition

See the controller's config/ kustomize tree for the CRD + RBAC + sample CR.

docs.title: Core (shared library)
docs.text:
Repo: secrets-bridge/core · Stack: Go 1.24, infra-free

Shared types + the provider interface every other Go service depends on. Deliberately small: adding anything Postgres-shaped or Redis-shaped here is a CI failure on the dependent repos.

docs.title: What lives in core
docs.text: Package Purpose providers/ The Provider interface, SecretRef / SecretMetadata / SecretValue / SecretVersion / PutOptions / ProviderScope, concurrent Registry, plus the Vault + AWS Secrets Manager connector packages sync/ Doc-only placeholder (the sync engine lives in the agent + worker; this package is reserved) types/ Doc-only placeholder

docs.title: The metadata / value split
docs.text:
type Provider interface {
    GetMetadata(ctx, ref) (SecretMetadata, error)        // CP, discovery, controller
    ListMetadata(ctx, scope) ([]SecretMetadata, error)
    GetValue(ctx, ref) (SecretValue, error)              // agent only
    PutValue(ctx, ref, value, opts) (SecretVersion, error) // agent only
}

The interface is the load-bearing architectural decision in the whole project. The CP only ever needs metadata; the agent only ever needs values. Different processes hold different trust.

SecretValue.String() and .GoString() both return "<redacted>", verified across every default formatting verb in core#3, so a casual log.Printf("%+v", value) can't leak.

docs.title: What core deliberately doesn't have
docs.text:
• No database/sql import
  • No github.com/redis/... import
  • No HTTP framework dependency
  • No knowledge of workflow / RBAC / audit (those live in the api)

If you find yourself wanting to add any of these, your code belongs in api or agent instead.

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
Repo: secrets-bridge/gateway · Stack: Go 1.26, stdlib net/http, log/slog, Prometheus client · Container: golang:1.26-alpine → distroless/static:nonroot, published as ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/gateway, signed with cosign and shipped with an SBOM and build provenance (verifying releases) · Chart: oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-gateway

The control plane decides, the agent executes, and the Gateway observes. A Gateway runs inside your security boundary, reads the state of the Argo CD Applications you list in its local configuration, and reports that state to the control plane as metadata. It never changes anything, and it is optional.

Release 1 is in progress

The Gateway binary, its Helm chart, the control-plane registry and the observation path (tasks, leases, results, evidence, verdicts, the worker sweepers and the console pages) are merged. Release 1 has not passed QA.

The control plane's own Argo CD poller (SB_GITOPS_ENABLED on the api and SB_WORKER_GITOPS_ENABLED on the worker, see GitOps observation) still exists until the cutover in gateway#13 ships. Each environment uses one observation source at a time: the control plane's poller, the Gateway, or none.

docs.title: Where it sits
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph cp ["Control plane: decides"]
        API["api<br/>policy, approvals,<br/>Gateway registry, audit"]
        PG[("Postgres")]
        API <--> PG
    end

    subgraph boundary ["Your boundary"]
        Agent["Agent: executes<br/>provider reads and writes"]
        GW["Gateway: observes<br/>optional, read-only"]
        Provider[("Secret provider")]
        Argo["Argo CD"]
    end

    Agent -->|"outbound HTTPS<br/>X-Agent-Secret"| API
    GW -->|"outbound HTTPS<br/>X-Gateway-Secret"| API
    Agent -->|"read and write values"| Provider
    GW -->|"GET only<br/>applications, get"| Argo

The agent and the Gateway each open their own outbound HTTPS connection to the control plane. There is no connection between them in either direction, and the agent does not depend on the Gateway. The control plane never connects into your network on the Gateway path.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Property What it means in the code Optional Governance and execution work without a Gateway. By design, a request with no Gateway observing it shows as unverified, never as failed. Outbound only The only listener is /healthz, /readyz and /metrics on a loopback address (127.0.0.1:8091 by default). A non-loopback address, including localhost, is refused at boot. Read-only Argo CD is read through a GET-only transport. The control-plane client can reach only the Gateway endpoints. No sync, rollback, refresh or patch is possible. Metadata only It reports sync status and revision, health, the last operation phase and the reconcile time. It never decodes Helm values, condition messages or health messages, and it reads no Kubernetes Secrets. Bound connectors only Connectors and targets come from a local file. The control plane names only a connector id and a target id. It cannot point the Gateway at a new host, project or Application. Stateless No database, no Redis, no volume. Several replicas share one Gateway identity.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
Argo CD Healthy and Synced, or a finished sync, are operational state. They are not proof that a new secret value reached a running workload: a secret change does not change Git, so an Application can be healthy and synced while its pods still hold the old value. The Argo CD connector reports at most observed with confidence low, attaches the caveat argocd_health_not_proof to every observation that is not an error. The control plane never turns it into a verified verdict: a task that saw only Argo CD Healthy and Synced ends unverified with the reason context_only.

A Gateway that is offline, not deployed or not yet bound means the observation is pending, and timed_out once the deadline passes. It never means the deployment is healthy, and it never fails the request. There is no failed verdict. Execution and approvals do not wait for it.

The Gateway is not an execution path. It does not call the agent, receive values or wraps, or hold provider credentials.

docs.title: Release 1 scope
docs.text:
Release 1 is Argo CD rollout-state observation only (gateway#12).

  • The supported connector kind is argocd. It reads one Application by name with GET /api/v1/applications/{name} (with ?appNamespace= when the target sets one) and checks its token at boot with GET /api/v1/session/userinfo. Nothing else.
  • With only argocd connectors, the Gateway reads no Kubernetes API. It builds no Kubernetes client, needs no service-account token and no RBAC, and runs no Kubernetes self-check.
  • The eso (External Secrets Operator) and rollout (Deployment rollout) connectors are Release 2. Their code is in the repo, but the Gateway refuses a connectors file that names them unless SB_GATEWAY_ENABLE_R2_CONNECTORS=true is set. That switch is not supported for production, and the Gateway logs a WARN at boot while it is on. The Helm chart does not render these kinds and never sets the switch.

What the Argo CD connector proposes for the stage argocd_context (the control plane recomputes every outcome from the reported facts):

Outcome When observed, confidence low The Application is Healthy and Synced, with no operation or a Succeeded one, and was reconciled after the change not_observed Anything else, including Progressing, Degraded, OutOfSync, a failed operation, or state reconciled at or before the change. Degraded is context, not a failure of the secret change unverifiable The Application is outside the AppProjects allowed in the local configuration. No status is reported error Argo CD cannot be read. A fixed error code, never a message

docs.title: Observation flow
docs.text:
Each environment has an observation source: control_plane (the default), gateway or none. When a change reaches executed, the control plane reads that source once and starts exactly one observer. A request never gets both a control-plane GitOps observation and a Gateway task.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Agent
    participant CP as Control plane
    participant GW as Gateway
    participant Argo as Argo CD
    participant UI as Request page
    Agent->>CP: job complete, request reaches executed
    CP->>CP: environment source is gateway
    CP->>CP: one task per matching binding, queued
    Note over CP: first claim allowed 10s later (not_before)
    GW->>CP: POST /gateways/:id/tasks/claim
    CP-->>GW: task with attempt_id, lease 60s, deadline
    GW->>Argo: GET /api/v1/applications/{name}
    Argo-->>GW: sync, health, operation, reconcile time
    opt work takes longer than the lease
        GW->>CP: POST /tasks/:task_id/lease
    end
    GW->>CP: POST /tasks/:task_id/result
    CP->>CP: check attempt, lease, schema, binding, time window
    CP->>CP: recompute stage outcome, compute verdict
    CP-->>GW: accepted, task_state, verdict, next
    UI->>CP: GET /requests/:id/observations
    CP-->>UI: rollup and stages, observed operational state
  1. Task. A patch or cross-team request that reaches executed in an environment whose source is gateway gets one task for each enabled binding that covers its secret scope, where the Gateway is not revoked or disabled, the Argo CD connector is approved and the bound target is still advertised. Release 1 tasks carry one stage, argocd_context. The first claim is allowed 10 seconds after executed. The deadline is the binding's observation_timeout_seconds (default 1800), raised to cover the target's advertised refresh interval and progress deadline plus 5 minutes, and never more than 24 hours. With no matching binding, no task is created and the request shows "No observation configured".
  2. Claim. The Gateway claims for itself only. The task is chosen by the authenticated Gateway id, never by anything in the body. A claim leases one task to one replica with a new attempt_id and a 60-second lease (capped at the deadline). Each replica holds at most one task, and the Gateway at most max_inflight_tasks (default 20). Nothing to claim answers 204 with Retry-After: 5.
  3. Lease. The Gateway renews the lease while it works, or releases the task early with a reason (shutdown, over_capacity, connector_unavailable). A release is never a failure. A lease that runs out puts the task back in the queue, and the old attempt_id can no longer renew, release or post a result.
  4. Result. The result is accepted only for the attempt the control plane dispatched to that Gateway, while its lease is live and before the deadline. The evidence must name the connector and target in the task, that connector must be approved and belong to the Gateway, the binding must still be live in the request's own environment and project, and the reported Application must be the object the target advertises. The schema is closed: unknown or duplicate keys are refused. Timestamps must fall inside the attempt, allowing for clock skew. A repeated result with the same body returns the stored answer (duplicate); a different body for the same attempt is a conflict.
  5. Verdict. The control plane recomputes the stage outcome from the reported facts and does not take the Gateway's word for it. Evidence, the task state, the verdict and the audit events are written in one transaction. A stage that is not yet observed puts the task back in the queue with a backoff of 15, 30, 60 and then 120 seconds until the deadline.

What the verdicts mean in Release 1:

Verdict Reason When pending The task is open (queued or leased) unverified context_only Argo CD was Healthy and Synced, idle or Succeeded, and reconciled after the change. This is observed operational state, so the verdict stays unverified unverified no_stage_observed The stage ended unverifiable, for example an Application outside the allowed AppProjects unverified gateway_errors Five Gateway-reported errors or refused attempts. The task is dead unverified superseded_by_later_write, source_changed, binding_removed A later change to the same secret, a change of the environment's source away from gateway, or a deleted binding cancelled the open task timed_out gateway_unavailable The deadline passed and the Gateway was not seen since the task was created, or is not active timed_out deadline_reached The deadline passed while the Gateway was up, for example while Argo CD stayed Progressing or OutOfSync

verified and partially_observed exist in the schema for the Release 2 stages (eso_sync, workload_rollout). A Release 1 task never reaches them. There is no failed verdict, so a Gateway that is offline or late leaves the request pending and then timed_out, never failed.

Revoking or disabling a Gateway moves its leased tasks back to queued and refuses the old attempts. A disabled Gateway can be enabled again; a revoked one cannot. Tasks it can no longer claim end timed_out at their deadline.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
The Gateway fails closed. Where it cannot prove a rule holds, it refuses to start, stops claiming, or stays not ready.

Rule How it holds GET only to Argo CD Each Argo CD client is pinned to the scheme and host of its base_url and allows GET to two paths. Every other method, path and query key is refused before the request leaves the process. resource-tree, managed-resources, manifests and the application list are blocked even though Argo CD's applications, get permission allows them, and so is ?refresh=, which would make Argo CD patch the Application. Redirects are refused, proxy variables are ignored, and responses are capped at 2 MiB. Least-privilege Argo CD account The token needs applications, get and nothing else. It is mounted as a file and re-read when it rotates. No Secrets access, ever Release 1 has no Kubernetes access at all. For the Release 2 Kubernetes connectors, a boot self-check refuses to start if the service account can use any verb on secrets, or any write verb on a resource a connector reads. A failed review call also refuses the boot. There is no override. The check repeats every 5 minutes and stops the Gateway if a grant appears. Writes only to the control plane The control-plane client refuses any method or path other than the Gateway endpoints, uses no proxy and never follows redirects. Enrollment refuses any URL that is not https. Credential at rest The control plane stores a SHA-256 hash of the Gateway secret and compares it in constant time. On the Gateway side the identity is a read-only file. A file that other users can read, or that its group can write, is refused at boot. Revocation After a revoke, the next heartbeat or catalog upload gets 401. The Gateway stops claiming and stays up and not ready, with the reason in its log, so the pod does not restart-loop. Separate identity Gateways have their own tables, header and middleware. An agent credential cannot authenticate as a Gateway, and a Gateway credential cannot reach agent routes.

Gateway evidence is customer-side attestation: whoever controls a Gateway can report false state for their own requests. The design accepts that for Release 1 by labelling evidence "observed by Gateway X". Signed evidence (gateway#7) must ship before Gateway evidence is presented as compliance evidence.

docs.title: Runtime behaviour
docs.text:
• A replica is ready when the control plane has accepted a recent heartbeat and the catalog, and every connector self-check passes.
  • Claiming pauses while no heartbeat has been accepted within SB_GATEWAY_CP_UNREACHABLE_AFTER (default 2m), the catalog is not accepted, or a connector is unverified. It resumes once all three hold again.
  • A 401 or an unsupported contract version stops claiming and leaves the process up and not ready.
  • gateway healthcheck is the client for the exec probes, since the image has no shell or curl and the local server listens on loopback only. It sends one GET to /readyz (or /healthz with --live) and exits 0 on a 200.

docs.title: Worker
docs.text:
Repo: secrets-bridge/worker · Stack: Go 1.25 + api/pkg/storage + api/pkg/runtime (via local replace directive) + Prometheus client · Container: golang:1.25-alpine → distroless/static:nonroot

Background workhorse for the platform's lifecycle hygiene + the read-only ArgoCD observation poller (BRD §26).

docs.title: Sweepers shipped today
docs.text: Name Cadence Job wraps-expired 60s Delete secret_wraps past expires_at secrets-stale 5m Flip discovered secrets rows whose last_seen_at < cutoff to status='missing' agents-stale 60s Flip agents whose last_seen_at < cutoff to status='stale' jobs-recovery 30s Mark sync_jobs rows whose claim lease expired without a complete as status='expired' discover-scheduler 5m Enqueue one discover job per configured target (env var today; admin API tracked) gitops-poller 15s Claim a queued observation → call ArgoCD → record observed_state → transition gitops-timeout 60s Flip observations past their timeout_at to applied_unverified observation-leases 30s Put Gateway observation tasks whose lease ran out back to queued. Opt-in with SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED observation-deadlines 30s Close open observation tasks past their deadline as timed_out (deadline_reached or gateway_unavailable), never failed. Opt-in gateways-stale 1m Flip Gateways with no heartbeat for SB_WORKER_GATEWAYS_STALE_AFTER (2m) from active to stale. Opt-in gateway-replicas-prune 1h Delete Gateway replica rows not seen for 24h. Opt-in users-pending 1m Post one webhook message about accounts newly waiting for approval, by email only. Registered only when SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_URL is set

docs.title: Multi-replica safety
docs.text:
Every sweeper acquires a Redis lock before running:

lock := scheduler.AcquireLock("worker:sweeper:" + name)
if errors.Is(err, runtime.ErrLockHeld) { /* metric, return */ }
// run + StartRenewal + Release on tick end

So you can scale the worker deployment to N replicas; exactly one runs each sweeper per tick, the others record worker_scheduler_lock_skipped_total (a metric, not a warn-level log, because N-1 of N replicas always skip).

docs.title: Notification sinks
docs.text: Sink Status Notes NoOp default Logs at the event's severity Webhook ships JSON POST; FormatSlack=true switches to {text: ...} envelope. 4xx is permanent (no retry); 5xx is transient (with backoff). Fanout ships errors.Join across N sinks; one bad sink doesn't block siblings Native Slack placeholder Tracked as a follow-up Email / SMTP placeholder PagerDuty placeholder

docs.title: Hard rules
docs.text:
• Stateless (NFR-08): all state in Postgres + Redis
  • No secret values logged or notified. Sweeper errors carry counts + cutoffs + sweeper names, never row contents. The one exception is users-pending, whose message lists the emails of waiting accounts. It goes to the webhook only, and the worker logs counts only
  • No provider SDKs imported (worker doesn't fetch values; the agent does)
  • Multi-replica safe by construction
  • Fails loud on misconfig at boot (e.g. SB_DISCOVER_TARGETS_JSON parse error → exit 1)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Env var Required Default Notes DATABASE_URL yes - Same Postgres as the api REDIS_URL yes - Same Redis as the api SB_WORKER_GITOPS_ENABLED no false Must match the api's SB_GITOPS_ENABLED for §26 to be active SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED no false Turns on the four Gateway observation sweepers. Their intervals are in the Configuration reference SB_DISCOVER_TARGETS_JSON no - Array of {agent_id, provider, config, scope}; admin API replaces this Sweeper interval overrides no per-sweeper defaults SB_WORKER_WRAPS_EXPIRED_INTERVAL, etc. See Configuration reference

docs.title: Design system
docs.text:
One system covers the console, this site and the brand marks. It aims for an operations tool written by the engineers who answer for it: plain, exact and quiet, with one ultramarine accent and nothing decorative.

Read these before you write copy, build a page or make an image:

  1. Brand voice: how we describe the product and its maturity, and the words we avoid.
  2. Tokens and theme: colours for light and dark, the type scale, spacing, radii, and where each repo reads them.
  3. Logos and assets: the Checkpoint mark, its approved colourings, the product icons and the architecture illustration.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text: Question Answer Name Secrets Bridge, two words, everywhere. In logos it comes from the lockup files; never retype it. Fonts IBM Plex Sans for what people read, IBM Plex Mono for what machines read (refs, key names, paths, times, code). Weights 400, 500 and 600. Accent Ultramarine #3141C8 on light, periwinkle #9AA3FF on dark. A signal only: links, one primary button per view, the current tab, the focus ring. Surfaces Paper bg, white surface, ink text. Panels separate with a border, not a shadow. Corners Square. 4 px is the largest radius. Only avatars are round. Status A small square and the exact status word. Colour never carries a status alone. Secret values Never shown outside the reveal panel: no values, lengths, hashes or previews.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• The console reads the tokens from src/index.css in the ui repo (Tailwind @theme), with light and dark themes.
  • This site maps the same tokens onto mkdocs-material in docs/stylesheets/brand.css.
  • Logos, icons and the illustration are served from this site's assets/ folder, listed on Logos and assets.

If something here doesn't cover your case, open an issue in secrets-bridge/docs and we'll either extend the system or write down the exception.

docs.title: The Checkpoint mark
docs.text:
Two squares joined by a route that turns once at a ring. Use the files below; never redraw the mark or retype the wordmark.

  • Use the horizontal lockup (mark and wordmark) by default, the mark alone in square spaces, and the favicon form below 20 px.
  • Approved colourings: ultramarine on bg or surface; periwinkle (accent dark) with light ink on dark; white on ultramarine; black; white.
  • Clear space is ⅜ of the mark height on every side.
  • Trademark clearance has not been checked.
File Use logo-horizontal-color.svg Lockup on light backgrounds (this site's header) logo-horizontal-dark.svg Lockup on dark backgrounds logo-mark.svg Mark alone, light backgrounds logo-mark-dark.svg Mark alone, dark backgrounds favicon.svg Browser tabs and anything under 20 px apple-touch-icon.png iOS home screen (180 px) og-banner.png Social cards (1200 × 630)

docs.title: Product icons
docs.text:
Four icons on a 24 px grid, 1.75 stroke, mitred joins, butt ends, one colour: request, approval, agent and audit. Inline them as SVG so they take currentColor.

File Meaning icon-request.svg A request icon-approval.svg An approval icon-agent.svg The agent icon-audit.svg The audit log

Right angles and 45° only; no curves except the checkpoint ring. No padlocks, shields, keys, clouds or circuit traces. No emoji.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
The architecture illustration (light, dark) follows the diagram rules:

  • Arrows point away from the side that opens the connection; solid opens, dashed returns.
  • The control plane has an accent-soft fill with an accent edge. Customer infrastructure has a dashed edge outline.
  • Providers connect only to the agent. Never draw a line from a provider to a browser or the console. Name providers in text; don't draw their logos.

Documentation diagrams use Mermaid, not screenshots.

docs.title: Brand voice
docs.text: Write the way the engineer who has to defend the claim in a review would.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Say what we keep. "We don't keep your secret values. We keep requests, approvals and audit metadata." Never "zero-knowledge" or "bank-grade".
  • Describe the mechanism. "The agent connects out, so you open no inbound ports." Not "seamless connectivity".
  • Label maturity exactly. Use the words on Product status: implemented, QA-certified, in progress, roadmap. Not "production-ready".
  • Short sentences, plain verbs, sentence case. "Ask for access. Someone approves. The agent reads it." No exclamation marks, no emoji.
  • No proof we don't have. No invented customers, certifications, percentages or uptime.
  • Address the reader as "you". Name people and teams: "Waiting for Sam Noor", not "Pending approval".
  • Errors say what happened and what to do. "That code wasn't accepted. Nothing was retrieved."

docs.title: Describing the product
docs.text: Where Wording One line Secrets Bridge governs who may use the secrets a team already keeps in AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault. A little more It adds access requests, approvals, audit and agent execution around those secrets. It keeps requests, approvals and audit metadata; the values stay in your provider. Providers Name the ones that work today. Azure Key Vault and GCP Secret Manager are on the roadmap; say so when you mention them. Maturity Open source and pre-1.0. Link to Product status rather than restating it.

docs.title: Words we avoid
docs.text: seamless, effortless, military-grade, bank-grade, unbreakable, guaranteed, revolutionary, zero-knowledge, production-ready, SOC 2-ready (or any certification we don't hold).

docs.text:

docs.text:
The console, this site and the brand assets use one set of tokens with light and dark values. Take every colour, size, radius and font from here; never copy a hex value out of a screenshot.

docs.text:
Build every screen from bg, surface, ink, muted, border and rule: roughly 70% bg, 13% surface, 10% ink, 5% muted and rule, and about 2% accent.

docs.text:
Everything you need to run Secrets Bridge.

docs.title: Production deployment
docs.text:
Install with the Helm charts from the charts repo. Both publish as OCI artifacts on GHCR:

Chart OCI reference What it installs secrets-bridge oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge api, ui, worker and controller behind one Ingress, in the control-plane cluster secrets-bridge-agent oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-agent One outbound-only agent per workload cluster or account secrets-bridge-gateway oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-gateway Optional. One read-only Gateway per boundary for Argo CD observation (Gateway, Release 1 in progress)

Images publish to ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/ as well. Until the first v0.1.0 release, chart versions look like 0.0.1-dev.<sha>; pin an exact version from the package list.

The chart defaults are the hardened baseline, so keep them rather than writing your own Deployments: non-root pods with read-only root filesystems, NetworkPolicies on by default, minimal RBAC, and render-time guards. helm install fails before anything starts when kms.backend=local is combined with env=production, when env or kms.backend is unknown, when a production image resolves to a mutable :dev or :latest tag without a digest, or when the agent's control-plane endpoint is plain http://.

# 1. Pre-create the env Secret the chart reads (secrets.existingSecret,
#    default name secrets-bridge-env): DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL and the
#    SB_KMS_* settings for your backend. Deliver it with
#    External Secrets, sealed-secrets or similar; never commit it.

# 2. Install the control plane. Production needs every image pinned.
helm install secrets-bridge oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --namespace secrets-bridge --create-namespace \
  --set ingress.host=secrets-bridge.example.com \
  --set kms.backend=aws-kms \
  --set kms.awsKms.region=us-east-1 \
  --set kms.awsKms.keyId=alias/sb-wrap \
  --set api.image.digest=sha256:<digest> \
  --set ui.image.digest=sha256:<digest> \
  --set worker.image.digest=sha256:<digest> \
  --set controller.image.digest=sha256:<digest>

Then onboard agents with the secrets-bridge-agent chart in enrollment mode; see Enrolling your first agent. Each chart's README in the charts repo documents every value.

Around the charts you provide:

  • A managed Postgres + Redis on a private network (we test against Postgres 17 + Redis 7)
  • A real KMS backend (vault-transit or aws-kms, never local outside dev)
  • An ingress controller with TLS and a real certificate

docs.title: Hardening checklist (before exposing to anyone)
docs.text:
• SB_ENV is production (the default), never dev
  • SB_KMS_BACKEND is vault-transit or aws-kms (never local)
  • None of the api's insecure switches are set: SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_HEADER_AUTH, SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT, SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_VAULT_ADDR, SB_MFA_DEV_ALLOW_PWD are unset or false, and SB_PROVIDER_CONN_REJECT_SECRETS is unset or true
  • SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT on the agent is unset (default is to refuse http://), and the chart's cp.insecureTransport is false
  • Agents are onboarded with one-time enrollment tokens, and their identity file sits on a persistent volume that only the agent mounts
  • TLS terminator (ingress) configured with HSTS + a real certificate
  • SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD is rotated immediately after first login
  • The admin user has a real OIDC identity assigned and the local admin is disabled (see Authentication)
  • Postgres is on a private network: the api + worker are the only clients
  • Redis is on a private network: the api + worker are the only clients
  • Audit-event shipping is configured (the schema-level append-only triggers are a defense, not a substitute for off-host log shipping)
  • Backup the KMS master key / Vault Transit key / AWS CMK: it's the only thing that can unwrap your envelopes

See the Threat model for the attacker postures these defend against.

docs.title: Agent onboarding
docs.text: An agent runs inside your boundary (a Kubernetes cluster, a VPC, an account) and talks outbound only to the control plane and its local provider. Onboarding is self-enrollment: an admin issues a short-lived, one-time token; the agent exchanges it for a persistent credential exactly once.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Admin
    participant CP as Control Plane
    participant Agent
    Admin->>CP: Create one-time enrollment token<br/>(bound to a provider connection)
    CP-->>Admin: enrollment_token (returned once, hash-only at rest)
    Admin->>Agent: deliver enrollment_token (via a Secret)
    Agent->>CP: POST /agents/enroll { enrollment_token, ... }
    CP-->>Agent: agent_token (returned ONCE) + agent_id
    Note over Agent: persist {agent_id, agent_token} safely<br/>(the token is spent, never reused)
    loop heartbeat
        Agent->>CP: POST /agents/:id/heartbeat (X-Agent-Secret)
        CP-->>Agent: 200 { next_heartbeat_seconds }
    end
    Admin->>CP: Revoke agent (when needed)
    CP-->>Agent: subsequent heartbeats / job polls rejected

docs.title: What happens, step by step
docs.text:
1. Admin creates a one-time enrollment token, bound to a specific provider connection. The token is short-lived, stored hash-only, and returned exactly once.
  2. The agent calls POST /agents/enroll with the token (the token travels in the request body, never a header, never a log line).
  3. The control plane returns a persistent agent_token once and creates the agent, bound to that provider connection.
  4. The agent stores its identity safely and, on restart, reuses it, it never spends a second enrollment token.
  5. The agent heartbeats using the X-Agent-Secret header; the control plane drives the cadence.
  6. An admin can revoke the agent at any time; its heartbeats and job polling stop being accepted immediately.

docs.title: Safety properties
docs.text:
• One-time tokens, hash-only at rest, short TTL, returned once, consumed once. Reuse is refused (409).
  • Provider-bound, an enrolled agent is tied to a single provider connection.
  • Outbound-only, no inbound ports; no Postgres / Redis / Kubernetes-API dependency.
  • Metadata-only audit, enrollment, rejection, and revocation events record IDs, reasons, and timestamps; never the token or the agent credential.
  • Legacy direct mint is disabled by default, the older direct agent-mint endpoint is off unless explicitly enabled as a break-glass admin action; enrollment is the standard path.

Never expose credential material

Enrollment tokens and agent credentials are secrets. Deliver them through a Kubernetes Secret (or your secret-distribution mechanism), never as a plaintext value in configuration, a log line, a screenshot, or a commit.

For the exact commands (token creation, Helm install in enrollment mode), see Enrolling your first agent; for a local run, see Running locally with docker compose. See the agent component reference and the HTTP API endpoints for the exact contract.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Secrets Bridge has three ways to sign in: an OIDC provider set with SB_OIDC_* environment variables, Google configured from the console, and the local password, which stays available as break-glass. It gates Tier 2 operations (approve, reject, reveal) behind fresh MFA. This page explains the model end-to-end so an operator knows what's enforced where.

docs.title: The session model (Slices A2 + C)
docs.text:
Sessions are server-side, not stateless tokens.

Concept Where it lives Identity proof sb_session cookie, HttpOnly, Secure (prod), SameSite=Strict Source of truth sessions table in Postgres, revoked_at, expires_at, idle_expires_at, last_mfa_at, ip, user_agent Cookie content 32 random bytes, base64url; SHA-256 stored, plaintext returned ONCE in Set-Cookie Revocation Immediate, UPDATE sessions SET revoked_at = NOW(); next request fails validation

The SPA never holds a token. Closing the tab + reopening it re-uses the same cookie. Reload, navigate, refresh, all hit the server. There is no localStorage / sessionStorage keypair to steal.

docs.title: TTLs (architect Q3)
docs.text:
TTL Default Behaviour Absolute 8 hours Hard ceiling from session create; the browser drops the cookie at this point Idle 30 minutes Slides forward on every authenticated request; clamped to the absolute TTL Step-up 15 minutes last_mfa_at must be within this window for Tier 2 ops

A user who hasn't acted in 30 minutes is logged out idle-side; a user who's been active for 8 straight hours is logged out absolute-side. Both require a fresh login.

docs.title: Account lockout (Slice A1)
docs.text:
Five consecutive wrong-password attempts pin the account out for 15 minutes. State lives in Postgres (local_users.failed_login_count + locked_until), not Redis, a cache flush must not silently re-enable a locked account.

Even a correct password is rejected during the lock window. The 6th attempt with the right password fails just like the wrong ones, operators must wait out the timer or have a sibling admin clear the lock via psql.

The audit trail captures every state change:

  • auth.login with status=denied + error_kind=wrong_password + failed_login_count=N, every wrong attempt
  • auth.lockout.applied, written exactly once, when the threshold is crossed
  • auth.login with status=denied + error_kind=account_locked, every attempt against a locked account
  • auth.login with status=success + BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN (severity=CRITICAL), successful sign-in, see below

docs.title: Rate limit (per-IP, anti-scan)
docs.text:
Endpoint Limit Window POST /auth/login 30 60s GET /auth/oidc/callback 60 60s GET /auth/providers 120 60s GET /auth/sso/google/start 30 60s GET /auth/sso/google/callback 60 60s POST /auth/oidc/{logout,backchannel} 60 60s POST /agents/:id/heartbeat 6 per-agent 60s GET /requests/:id/wraps/:wrap_id 20 per-user 60s

The login / callback caps are deliberately permissive so users behind shared CGNAT (an entire ISP or VPC behind one egress IP) aren't locked out by their neighbours. Brute-force defence lives in the per-account lockout above, not the per-IP rate limit, the lockout is IP-independent so rotating source IPs doesn't dodge it. Tuned for carrier-grade NAT and other shared-egress networks.

docs.title: OIDC sign-in (Slices B + C + E)
docs.text:
One env-var Identity Provider (architect Q4). The api refuses to mount the /auth/oidc/* routes unless SB_OIDC_ISSUER is set; until then, only /auth/login (local password) and, when it is turned on, Google from the console accept sign-ins.

The flow:

SPA → GET /api/v1/auth/oidc/start
api → 302 to IdP with PKCE state/nonce/code_challenge
IdP → user authenticates + consents
IdP → 302 back to /api/v1/auth/oidc/callback?code=...&state=...
api → verify state, exchange code, verify ID token (signature + audience + nonce)
api → JIT upsert local_users row keyed on email-or-sub
api → reconcile user_roles against the configured group claim (see below)
api → stamp last_mfa_at if amr ⊇ {strong-factor}
api → Set-Cookie + 302 to return_to
SPA → /users/me → render

docs.title: Group-claim → role mapping (Slice E)
docs.text:
SB_OIDC_GROUP_MAP is a JSON object mapping IdP group names to Secrets Bridge role names:

{
  "sb-admins":    "admin",
  "sb-approvers": "approver",
  "sb-devs":      "developer"
}

The reconciler runs on every OIDC sign-in:

  • User has a mapped group → grant added (if absent), granted_by='system:oidc'
  • User no longer has a mapped group → grant revoked
  • Mapped role doesn't exist in the catalog → silent skip + audit (typo doesn't 5xx the login)
  • Reconcile failure → audited as auth.oidc.reconcile_failed; user still signs in

docs.title: The reconciler invariant (don't break this)
docs.text:
The reconciler only touches user_roles rows with granted_by = 'system:oidc'.

Admin-assigned grants, the SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USER_ID grant, every manually-curated team-scoped grant, every grant created via POST /api/v1/user-roles, carry a different granted_by value and are invisible to the reconciler. They survive every reconcile pass, including the "user belongs to no mapped groups" case.

This protects:

  1. The break-glass admin from getting locked out when the IdP returns no groups during an outage.
  2. Manually-curated team-scoped grants (which OIDC has no way to express in v1).
  3. Operator overrides during incident response.

If you ever find yourself "cleaning up" this filter, stop. It is the security boundary, not an accident.

docs.title: Google sign-in from the console
docs.text:
Separate from the env-var provider above, an admin with auth.sso.edit can connect a Google Workspace under Admin → Sign-in, with no restart. Its accounts are bound by Google's issuer and subject rather than by email, the ID token's hd claim must be in the allowed Workspace domains, and new accounts wait for an admin's approval by default. Existing accounts connect Google from their profile after a fresh second factor. Both providers can be configured at once; the login page shows a button for each.

See Sign in with Google for setup, approvals and the audit events.

docs.title: MFA + step-up (Slices H + I, current model)
docs.text:
Tier 2 operations (approve / reject / reveal-wrap; future: rotate, role-edit, provider-edit) require a session whose last_mfa_at is within the step-up TTL.

The Control Plane owns MFA enrollment + step-up directly. Identity stays with the IdP; MFA is an app-level concern. This is an architectural inversion of the original Slice D design (described as the legacy path further down). Every user enrolls one or more factors in the SPA at /me/mfa; step-up runs through the api's /auth/mfa/{challenge,verify} endpoints. Local-admin and OIDC users follow the same enrollment surface and the same step-up flow.

docs.title: Factor types
docs.text:
Kind Library on the api side Description totp stdlib (RFC 6238, HMAC-SHA1, 6 digits, 30 s step, ±1 step skew) Compatible with every authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Bitwarden, YubiKey Authenticator). webauthn github.com/go-webauthn/webauthn (FIDO2 / WebAuthn) Hardware-backed: YubiKey, Solo, Titan, platform authenticators (Touch ID / Face ID / Windows Hello). Phishing-resistant by design.

WebAuthn requires the chart's api.config.mfa.webauthn.rpId + api.config.mfa.webauthn.rpOrigins to be set. When either is empty the api mounts only the TOTP routes (and the SPA's /me/mfa page hides the "Add security key" button). See Configuration reference for the values.

docs.title: Enrollment ceremony
docs.text:
Both kinds follow the same two-step shape (Stripe / GitHub / AWS Console model):

  1. POST /users/me/mfa/<kind>/.../start mints the challenge + envelope-encrypts the factor secret + parks the encrypted blob in Redis under a 10-minute challenge id. Nothing lands in Postgres yet.
  2. POST /users/me/mfa/<kind>/.../confirm (or …/finish) consumes the Redis blob (GETDEL, single-shot), verifies the user's response, and only then persists the factor row.

A wrong TOTP code or a failed WebAuthn attestation burns the challenge, the user restarts from step 1. This blocks an attacker from brute-forcing the 6-digit space against a single secret.

The SPA exposes the enrollment surfaces at /me/mfa. A user with zero factors sees an accent-coloured "Add MFA factor →" nudge in the sidebar; an enrolled user sees a quieter "Security" link.

docs.title: Step-up ceremony
docs.text:
When a Tier 2 op hits the api's RequireFreshMFA gate on a stale session:

401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: step-up max_age=900 acr_values=mfa

The SPA's global onError interceptor opens the step-up modal:

  1. Modal asks the user to pick a factor, filtered by what they have enrolled.
  2. SPA calls POST /auth/mfa/challenge { kind } for the chosen kind.
  3. TOTP path, user types the 6-digit code; SPA calls POST /auth/mfa/verify { challenge_id, factor_id, code }.
  4. WebAuthn path, SPA calls navigator.credentials.get(...) with the api-issued options; ships the assertion back via POST /auth/mfa/verify { challenge_id, response }.
  5. On 204 No Content the session is MFA-fresh, the api stamped last_mfa_at on the same session row (no new cookie). The user re-clicks the original button.

docs.title: Two related responses the interceptor routes
docs.text: Response What it means SPA action 412 mfa_enrollment_required User has zero factors enrolled. Navigate to /me/mfa. The step-up modal would be a dead-end. 401 factor_compromised WebAuthn sign-count regression, the api detected a possible cloned authenticator and revoked every session for the user. Hard-navigate to /login.

docs.title: Recommended factor priority
docs.text:
When you onboard users, encourage this enrollment order:

  1. WebAuthn (hardware key, YubiKey, Solo, Titan), phishing-resistant, no shared secret on the device, no battery.
  2. WebAuthn (platform, Touch ID / Face ID / Windows Hello), phishing-resistant, no extra device to carry, but tied to one machine.
  3. TOTP via authenticator app (Aegis, 1Password, Authy), universal fallback; vulnerable to phishing kits that proxy the code.
  4. SMS / email OTP, Secrets Bridge does NOT support this. SIM swap and email-account takeover are well-documented bypasses.

Operators should enrol at least two factors per privileged user, one hardware key plus one TOTP backup, so a lost YubiKey doesn't lock them out of Tier 2 ops.

docs.title: Step-up vs login-time MFA
docs.text:
The default posture (Slices H + I) gates only Tier-2 ops (approve / reject / reveal-wrap). Sign-in itself + Tier-1 browsing (lists, dashboards) only need a session cookie. The argument: the session cookie is the high-value loot, step-up makes "I have your cookie" insufficient at the moment of a sensitive action without paying the ergonomic cost of a modal on every page load.

The alternative posture, login-time MFA on every authenticated route, is available via the Slice K opt-in knob.

Set api.config.mfa.requireMFAAtLogin: true (renders SB_REQUIRE_MFA_AT_LOGIN=true) to enable. When the knob is on:

  • A fresh session with no MFA stamp returns 401 step_up_required on every Tier-1 route (lists, dashboards, project pages).
  • The SPA's global onError interceptor opens the step-up modal immediately after sign-in before the user reaches any value-bearing surface.
  • A user with no factor enrolled is bounced to /me/mfa via the 412 mfa_enrollment_required shape (the same response the existing 412 path uses).
  • Tier-2 routes still enforce the 15-min freshness window via the per-route RequireFreshMFA.

Carve-outs the gate ALWAYS allows through (so it isn't self-locking):

GET    /api/v1/users/me                 SPA identity hydration
GET    /api/v1/users/me/projects        identity-adjacent
GET    /api/v1/users/me/mfa/factors     SPA factor-kind picker
POST   /api/v1/users/me/mfa/totp/*      enrollment must reach
POST   /api/v1/users/me/mfa/webauthn/*  the user pre-stamp
DELETE /api/v1/users/me/mfa/factors/:id factor removal
POST   /api/v1/auth/logout              always allow sign-out
POST   /api/v1/auth/mfa/challenge       the gate's own ceremony
POST   /api/v1/auth/mfa/verify          ditto

Pick the posture by environment, not by user:

Posture When it fits Step-up only (default) Dev clusters, single-tenant deployments, deployments where users browse infrequently and verifying on every access would be friction without benefit. Login-time MFA (requireMFAAtLogin: true) Production multi-tenant deployments, regulated environments (SOC2 / ISO 27001 audit), AWS-Console / GitHub-org-with-2FA-required parity.

The two postures share the same factor enrollment surface (/me/mfa) and the same verify endpoint (/auth/mfa/verify), the gate position is the only difference. Switching between them is a single env-var change + pod roll; users keep their enrolled factors.

docs.title: OIDC-trust MFA (Slice D, legacy, opt-in)
docs.text:
The api retains the original Slice D path for deployments whose IdP genuinely owns MFA (Microsoft Entra / Okta with strong-factor policy bound), so an operator can keep that posture during a transition window.

Set api.config.oidc.trustAmrForMFA: true (renders SB_OIDC_TRUSTED_AMR_MFA=true) to opt in. When enabled, the OIDC callback stamps last_mfa_at on the session whenever the ID-token amr claim includes one of the RFC 8176 strong-factor identifiers:

Factor Code Multi-factor (explicit) mfa One-time password otp Hardware key hwk FIDO2 / WebAuthn fido Software-secured key swk Smart card sc Proof-of-possession pop Biometric, iris eye Biometric, fingerprint fpt Biometric, retina retina

pwd and kba are not strong. The app-MFA path (above) runs in parallel, a user can still satisfy step-up via /auth/mfa/verify even when the OIDC-trust knob is on. Operators flip this knob OFF (the default) once every user has enrolled an app-MFA factor; amr continues to be recorded in audit either way.

Hard rule: SessionService.MarkMFA only fires from MFAVerifyService.Verify (the app path) OR from the OIDC callback when TrustAMRForMFA=true. The architectural invariant is that exactly one path writes last_mfa_at. New callers in the api codebase need explicit justification or the step-up gate's contract collapses.

docs.title: Break-glass (local-admin) policy (architect Q1)
docs.text:
Local-admin sign-in via /auth/login is the break-glass surface, the way operators sign in when the IdP is down, the OIDC client is misconfigured, or the network is partitioned. It is not the day-to-day sign-in path once OIDC is configured.

Every successful local-admin sign-in emits a high-severity audit event:

action:   BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN
status:   success
severity: CRITICAL    (in metadata)
actor:    user:<uuid>

Route this audit action into your alert pipeline. Splunk / Datadog / Grafana Alertmanager, whichever you use, page the on-call when a BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN shows up outside of an open incident bridge. The Slack notification recipe:

# Example: worker notification sink (when configured) or external SIEM rule
when:
  action: BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN
  severity: CRITICAL
then:
  notify:
    channel: "#security-incidents"
    message: |
      Break-glass local-admin login by ${actor}.
      Expected? If not, open an incident.
      Session ID: ${metadata.session_id}
      IP: ${metadata.ip}
      User-agent: ${metadata.user_agent}

docs.title: Local-admin sessions + step-up
docs.text:
Local-admin users go through the same app-MFA enrollment + step-up surfaces as OIDC users. The local-admin sign-in path does not stamp last_mfa_at directly, every Tier 2 op the operator runs is gated by a fresh /auth/mfa/verify against an enrolled factor.

Operationally this means:

  • A local-admin user with no factor enrolled hits 412 mfa_enrollment_required on the first Tier 2 op and is routed to /me/mfa to enrol.
  • After enrolling, every Tier 2 op runs through the step-up modal, same flow as OIDC users.
  • If the operator is in the middle of an IdP outage and also hasn't enrolled an MFA factor, they should enrol one immediately, the IdP outage doesn't block factor enrollment, and once enrolled they can satisfy step-up without the IdP.

This is a tighter posture than the pre-H4 architecture, where local-admin users were forced through /auth/oidc/start?step_up=mfa for every Tier 2 op and effectively couldn't approve anything during an IdP outage. App-MFA closes that gap.

If you're routinely approving as the break-glass user, your operating model is still wrong, that account should be reserved for "the IdP is broken and I need to fix it." But during a real IdP outage the break-glass user can now approve cleanly without an additional dependency.

docs.title: Disabling break-glass entirely
docs.text: For deployments that want to refuse local-admin sign-in once OIDC is configured, the chart will gain a SB_LOCAL_ADMIN_ENABLED=false flag in a follow-up. Today the flag is implicit, leave SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL unset and no local-admin account exists, so /auth/login always fails with invalid credentials.

docs.title: Direct reveal permission (Slice L4)
docs.text:
Slice L4 added secret.reveal.direct to the permission catalog and seeded it onto the bootstrap developer role.

The permission is a NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT gate. Three conditions must all hold for a direct-reveal request to auto-execute:

  1. The caller holds secret.reveal.direct (route-level auth.Require).
  2. The matched policy_rules row has direct_reveal_allowed=true.
  3. The matched environment's kind is non_prod.

If any one of these fails, the API returns 403 and the SPA shows an inline error. The dev endpoint never bypasses approval against a prod-classified env, the PolicyEngine zeroes direct_reveal_allowed=true server-side regardless of operator misconfig. See Project environments for the kind model and Policy templates for ready-to-paste rules.

Operators who want a stricter baseline can strip secret.reveal.direct from the developer role via the existing Roles admin endpoint, the rest of the developer surface (secret.request, audit.read) is unaffected.

docs.title: What this page does NOT cover
docs.text:
• RBAC enforcement at the route level. Sidebar nav already hides admin pages without team.edit / role.edit; route-level enforcement on the api lands in a follow-up.
  • Audit log forwarding to SIEM. The api emits structured slog JSON; pick that up with Fluent Bit / Vector and route to wherever.
  • mTLS for agent ↔ api. Slice B of the workload-identity track replaces the static agent secret with a SPIFFE / IRSA-backed identity. Tracked separately from the user-auth series.

For the chart-side knobs (api.config.oidc.*, api.config.bootstrap.userId), see Configuration reference. For the underlying threat model + hard rules, see Threat model.

docs.title: Bootstrap & first sign-in
docs.text: After the api starts for the first time, the platform has to be bootstrapped with a usable admin identity. Otherwise nothing can be done: every write endpoint is gated by auth.Require(perm) and there are no role assignments yet.

docs.title: What "bootstrapped" means
docs.text:
Two things happen on first boot when local_users is empty and the bootstrap env vars are set:

  1. A local admin user is created, bcrypt-hashed password stored in local_users (idempotent: a second boot with the same env vars is a no-op once any user exists).
  2. The new user is bound to the seed admin role with global scope, via the existing user_roles flow.

The api logs both actions at INFO in its JSON log output:

{"msg":"bootstrap local admin created","user_id":"<uuid>","email":"admin@example.com"}
{"msg":"bootstrap admin assignment created","user_id":"<uuid>","role":"admin","scope":"global"}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Env var Required Default Notes SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL recommended on first boot Becomes the local-admin email SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD recommended on first boot Rotate immediately after first sign-in SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USER_ID optional Pre-OIDC escape hatch: assigns the admin role to a specific opaque user_id (matches the future OIDC sub claim). Use this alongside _EMAIL/_PASSWORD if you want both the local-admin login and a pre-arranged OIDC identity to hold admin.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text:
1. Open the UI (http://localhost:5173/ for the local docker compose setup).
  2. You'll be redirected to /login.
  3. Enter the email + password from the env vars (or a dev user from the api's first-boot log when it runs with SB_ENV=dev).
  4. You land on the Dashboard with the Agents Online KPI showing 0 / 0.

The api keeps you signed in with an HttpOnly session cookie, which the SPA's scripts can't read. Sign out from the console to end the session.

docs.title: Rotating the admin password
docs.text:
There's no UI surface for this in the current slice. For now, use psql directly against the api's Postgres:

# Generate a bcrypt hash for the new password
NEW_HASH=$(htpasswd -bnBC 12 "" "your-new-password" | tr -d ':\n' | sed 's/^.\$2y/$2y/')

# Update the row (local docker compose setup; use your own psql
# connection elsewhere)
docker compose exec -T postgres \
  psql -U secrets_bridge -d secrets_bridge \
  -c "UPDATE local_users SET password_hash = decode('$(echo "$NEW_HASH" | xxd -p)', 'hex') WHERE email = 'admin@example.com';"

A real password-change endpoint + UI page lands as a follow-up.

docs.title: Disabling the local admin (after OIDC ships)
docs.text:
Once you've added a real OIDC identity with the admin role, you can disable the local-admin row so brute-force attempts against its bcrypt hash are pointless:

UPDATE local_users SET disabled = TRUE WHERE email = 'admin@example.com';

A disabled user's login attempts return the same generic 401 invalid credentials; the audit log records error_kind=user_disabled.

docs.title: Enrolling your first agent
docs.text:
Agents onboard by enrollment. An admin creates a one-time token bound to a provider connection; the agent exchanges it once for a persistent identity and stores that identity itself. See Agent onboarding for the model.

The UI has no enrollment screen yet, so create the token through the API. You need agent.mint (the seed admin role has it) and an active provider connection.

CP=https://secrets-bridge.example.com   # http://localhost:8080 for the local setup

# Sign in. The password is read from the terminal and handed to jq on
# stdin (printf is a shell builtin), so it is never in a command line,
# the shell history or the process list. The session cookie goes into a
# private cookie jar.
JAR=$(mktemp) && chmod 600 "$JAR"
read -rp 'Admin email: ' SB_ADMIN_EMAIL
IFS= read -rsp 'Admin password: ' SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD; echo
printf '%s\n%s\n' "$SB_ADMIN_EMAIL" "$SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD" | jq -Rn '{email: input, password: input}' \
  | curl -fsS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/login" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @-

# Pick the provider connection the agent will serve.
curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections" \
  | jq '.[] | {id, name, type, cluster_name, status}'
CONN_ID=<provider-connection-id>

# Create the one-time token and put it straight into a Kubernetes Secret
# in the workload cluster, without printing it.
kubectl create namespace secrets-bridge   # skip if it already exists
curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections/$CONN_ID/agent-enrollment-token" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"cluster-a-agent","expected_cluster_name":"cluster-a","expected_provider_type":"vault"}' \
  | jq -j .enrollment_token \
  | kubectl -n secrets-bridge create secret generic secrets-bridge-agent-enrollment \
      --from-file=enrollment_token=/dev/stdin

All body fields are optional. expires_in_seconds defaults to 900 (15 minutes) and is clamped to 60 to 86400. When expected_cluster_name or expected_provider_type is set, an agent that reports anything else is refused. The response carries the token exactly once, so don't log or paste the whole response. Its install_hint commands don't contain the token: they read it at a silent prompt.

Then install the agent chart in enrollment mode (see Production deployment for the chart source):

helm install secrets-bridge-agent oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-agent \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --namespace secrets-bridge \
  --set clusterName=cluster-a \
  --set cp.endpoint=https://secrets-bridge.example.com \
  --set enrollment.enabled=true \
  --set enrollment.tokenSecretName=secrets-bridge-agent-enrollment \
  --set identity.mode=file \
  --set identity.persistence.enabled=true \
  --set agent.providerType=vault \
  --set providers.vault.enabled=true \
  --set providers.vault.addr=https://vault.example.com \
  --set providers.vault.kubernetesRole=secrets-bridge-agent

On first boot the agent calls POST /api/v1/agents/enroll with the token, writes {agent_id, agent_secret} to SB_IDENTITY_FILE on the persistent volume and starts heartbeating. Restarts reuse that file; the token is never spent twice. The agent shows up under GET /api/v1/provider-connections/<id>/agents and turns active on its first heartbeat.

If the agent fails to enroll (expired token, wrong cluster name or provider type), fix the cause and create a new token. An unused token stops working when it expires, so keep expires_in_seconds short.

Direct agent mint is a dev-only break-glass

The + Mint agent drawer on the Agents page and POST /api/v1/agents use the legacy direct mint, which hands back a long-lived agent_secret. The api refuses it with 403 direct_agent_mint_disabled unless it runs with SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT=true. Leave that switch off outside a local dev loop; see Insecure switches.

docs.title: Submitting your first read request
docs.text:
Once you have an agent running and provider creds configured for it:

  1. Sidebar → Requests → + New request
  2. Read type
  3. Provider: Vault (or AWS Secrets Manager)
  4. Project and Environment: the project and environment the secret is bound to. Environment is required when the binding is scoped to one
  5. Secret reference: e.g. prod/db/password
  6. Keys: e.g. DB_PASSWORD (or leave one empty row for "all keys in the bundle")
  7. Justification: required, typically an incident or ticket number
  8. Submit → you're navigated to the request detail page

Then sign in as a second user with the secret.approve permission and approve from the Requests page's Approver queue. The requester can never approve or reject their own request, whatever their role (admin included) or the workflow says: the api answers 403 separation_of_duties_violated and audits the attempt.

Once approved → agent claims → fetches → posts wrap → request → executed. Refresh the detail page; the Wraps card now shows DB_PASSWORD with the Reveal (one-time) button. Click it, confirm, see the value, copy it, close.

That's the whole read flow.

At least 5s SB_WORKER_OBSERVATION_DEADLINES_INTERVAL no 30s Tick of observation-deadlines, which closes open tasks past their deadline as timed_out.
