docs.title: gateway
docs.text:
The Gateway binary. Each variable also has a flag (gateway -h); a flag overrides its variable. A malformed value stops the boot instead of falling back to the default. The secrets-bridge-gateway chart sets these from its values, and the gateway README is the source for this table.

Env var Required Default Notes SB_CP_ENDPOINT yes https://cp.example.com. https:// only, unless SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true. No userinfo SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT no false Dev only: allows http:// to the control plane and to every Argo CD base_url. See Insecure switches SB_CP_CA_FILE no PEM bundle that replaces the system roots for the control plane SB_CP_TLS_SERVER_NAME no TLS server name override SB_GATEWAY_IDENTITY_FILE no /etc/secrets-bridge/gateway/identity.json {"gateway_id": "...", "gateway_secret": "..."} from enrollment. Mode 0400, 0600 or 0440 (what a Secret volume with fsGroup produces). Any bit for other users, or group write, is refused at boot SB_GATEWAY_ID / SB_GATEWAY_SECRET no Credential pair as env vars. When both are unset the identity file is read. The chart does not use them SB_GATEWAY_LOCAL_ADDR no 127.0.0.1:8091 /healthz, /readyz and /metrics. Must be a literal loopback IP; localhost is refused SB_GATEWAY_CONNECTORS_FILE no JSON list of locally bound connectors. Empty binds none. The chart renders it into a ConfigMap SB_GATEWAY_ENABLE_R2_CONNECTORS no false Binds the Release 2 eso and rollout kinds. Not supported for production: the Gateway logs a WARN at boot while it is on. When off, a connectors file that names either kind is refused. The chart never sets it SB_GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_GRACE no 15s Half is spent waiting for passes in flight, then unfinished tasks are released SB_GATEWAY_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL no 30s Used until the control plane suggests an interval SB_GATEWAY_CLAIM_INTERVAL no 5s Base claim interval, jittered between half and one and a half times SB_GATEWAY_CLAIM_IDLE_MAX no 30s Longest claim interval after empty polls. Not shorter than the claim interval SB_GATEWAY_CLAIM_CONCURRENCY no 1 Observation passes in flight per replica, 1 to 16 SB_GATEWAY_LEASE_MARGIN no 3s A pass stops this long before its lease expires SB_GATEWAY_PASS_TIMEOUT no 30s Upper bound for one pass SB_GATEWAY_CP_UNREACHABLE_AFTER no 2m The Gateway turns not ready when no heartbeat has been accepted for this long SB_LOG_LEVEL no info debug, info, warn or error

The Gateway ignores HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY for every connection, so a bearer credential never reaches a proxy.

Each entry in the connectors file has a name (a DNS label the control plane binds to), a kind and settings. For argocd the settings are base_url, token_file (an absolute path), optional ca_file, tls_server_name and timeout (1s to 60s, default 10s), allowed_projects (at least one AppProject) and applications (at least one {id, name, app_namespace?}). Unknown fields, unknown kinds and duplicate names are refused at load.

docs.title: Secret material, naming convention
docs.text:
Material What it is Where it lives Rotation SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY Master key for the local KMS backend api env / K8s Secret Don't use in production, use Vault Transit or AWS KMS SB_KMS_VAULT_TOKEN Vault token for the vault-transit backend api env / K8s Secret Lease-tracked; refresh via Vault rotation Agent identity (agent_id + agent_secret) Per-agent credential, sent as X-Agent-Secret SB_IDENTITY_FILE on a persistent volume (or SB_AGENT_ID / SB_AGENT_SECRET) Revoke the agent, create a new enrollment token, re-enroll with an empty identity file SB_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN One-time enrollment token K8s Secret, read on first boot Single use; expires after 15 minutes by default Gateway identity (gateway_id + gateway_secret) Per-Gateway credential, sent as X-Gateway-Secret An existing K8s Secret, mounted read-only as SB_GATEWAY_IDENTITY_FILE No rotation in Release 1: revoke the Gateway, create a new one, enroll it and update the Secret Gateway enrollment token One-time token from POST /api/v1/admin/gateways/:id/enrollment-token Used once from the operator's workstation, never stored in the cluster Single use; expires after 15 minutes by default Argo CD token for the Gateway Read-only token of a local Argo CD account (applications, get) An existing K8s Secret, mounted as a file per connector Update the Secret; the Gateway re-reads the file SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD Seed admin password api env at first boot Rotate immediately after first sign-in

None of these should ever appear in:

  • Git history (use a K8s Secret, sealed-secret, or external-secrets-operator binding)
  • CI logs (mask via the CI's secret-masking facility)
  • Docker images (env vars in Dockerfile ENV are baked into layers)
  • Application logs (the api strips them from all log lines)

docs.title: Insecure switches (dev only)
docs.text:
Never set any of these in production

Each switch below turns off a security control so a laptop dev loop works without TLS, a real KMS or MFA hardware. All of them default to the safe value. If you find one set on a shared or routable deployment, treat it as an incident.

Switch Component Default What the unsafe value does Guard SB_ENV=dev api production Allows the local KMS backend and SB_MFA_DEV_ALLOW_PWD, seeds three dev users with logged passwords on an empty database, and drops the Secure flag from session cookies Unknown values fail boot; WARN log at boot SB_KMS_BACKEND=local (with SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY) api local Keeps the storage-envelope master key in the api's own environment, next to the data it protects api refuses to boot unless SB_ENV=dev, so an unset backend fails closed in production; the secrets-bridge chart refuses kms.backend=local with env=production SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_HEADER_AUTH=true api false Accepts an X-User-Id header as the caller's identity when there is no session cookie. Anyone who can reach the api can act as any user. Not tied to SB_ENV; WARN log at boot SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT=true api false Re-enables POST /api/v1/agents, which creates an agent and returns a long-lived agent_secret outside the enrollment flow No boot-time WARN. While off, the route answers 403 direct_agent_mint_disabled SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_VAULT_ADDR=true api false Accepts http:// Vault addresses on provider connections WARN log at boot SB_ALLOW_UNSEALED_WRAPS=true api false Hands wraps to an agent with no X25519 public key on file as plaintext over TLS, and accepts a plaintext value when an agent posts a wrap. Only for an agent that predates wire-envelope sealing. WARN log at boot. While off, a keyless agent gets 409 agent_public_key_required before the wrap is consumed and a value post gets 400 envelope_required; both are audited SB_PROVIDER_CONN_REJECT_SECRETS=false api true Turns off the check that rejects secret-shaped values (AWS keys, Vault tokens, JWTs, OAuth tokens) in provider-connection scope. Credential-shaped key names are still refused. WARN log at boot SB_MFA_DEV_ALLOW_PWD=true api false Treats every live session as MFA-fresh, so step-up-gated actions (approve, reveal, role and provider edits) need only a password sign-in api refuses to boot unless SB_ENV=dev; WARN log at boot SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true agent false Allows a plain http:// control-plane endpoint, so the agent credential and job traffic cross the network unencrypted WARN log at boot; the agent chart refuses an http:// endpoint unless cp.insecureTransport=true SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true gateway false Allows plain http:// to the control plane and to every Argo CD endpoint, so the Gateway credential and the Argo CD token cross the network unencrypted WARN log at boot; the secrets-bridge-gateway chart refuses an http:// URL unless insecureTransport=true SB_GATEWAY_ENABLE_R2_CONNECTORS=true gateway false Binds the Release 2 eso and rollout connectors, which read the Kubernetes API. Not supported for production WARN log at boot. The Kubernetes self-check still refuses any access to Secrets. The gateway chart never sets it

The hardening checklist checks each of these before a deployment is exposed.

docs.title: Cross-team requests
docs.text:
A cross-team request is a value handoff between two teams that don't share direct access to each other's secrets. Team A owns a workload that needs a value. Team B owns the value. Team A submits the request; a Team B member fills it; a Team A approver (and, when policy requires it, a security approver) verifies; the agent writes the value into Team A's provider. The original Team B member never touches Team A's workload, and Team A never sees Team B's source of truth.

Cross-team requests are the safe alternative to "share me your prod secret" Slack messages. Every value handoff lands in the audit log with a justification, a workflow snapshot, and a separation-of-duties trail.

This page covers the operator-facing model: the state machine, the permission matrix, the workflow knobs you can tune, and the SQL + metrics you'll use to triage. The SPA flow is described from the user's point of view inline; the API contract is at HTTP API endpoints, Cross-team requests.

docs.title: Target vs destination
docs.text:
Every cross-team request carries two scopes. They look similar but mean opposite things, and operator queries get them confused often enough that we make the distinction here.

Scope Means Example Target (target_team_id + target_project_id + target_environment_id) The team / project / env that provides the value. Team B's territory. The inbox is computed against this. team-alpha / team-alpha-billing / prod Destination (destination_provider_connection_id + destination_secret_ref + destination_keys) Where the value lands after approval. Team A's territory. The agent writes here. vault-prod / tenant-a/web/db / ["DB_PASSWORD", "DB_USER"]

The destination provider connection MUST be bound to the source project (Team A's project). The submit endpoint rejects destination_provider_unbound if the provider connection doesn't belong to the source project. This is the architectural fence that keeps Team B from accidentally writing into Team A's neighbours.

Bindings are managed via the admin page documented at Provider connections, one connection per external store, then a (project, env) binding row per project that needs to consume it. The cross-team submit drawer's destination dropdown calls the same /provider-connections URL with project_id + environment_id set so the api returns only the sanitized {id, name, type} projection scoped to the caller's source project + env. When the dropdown is empty, the drawer branches the empty-state CTA on hasPermission('integration.edit'), admins see a "Manage provider connections" link, non-admins see "Ask your platform team to bind a provider connection." Cross-team submits against a disabled destination return 409 connection_disabled.

Two kinds of binding affect what shows up in the destination dropdown:

Binding shape Created by When it appears in the dropdown Env-specific (environment_id IS NOT NULL) Platform admins (integration.edit) OR scoped binders (integration.bind, EPIC Q) via the per-env Provider Connections card on /projects/:id/env/:env_id When the cross-team source project + env match Project-wide (environment_id IS NULL) Platform admins ONLY. Scoped binders cannot create or delete project-wide bindings When the cross-team source project matches, regardless of env

A project-wide binding implicitly covers every environment, including production, which is why the §2 lock keeps project-wide bindings as platform-only.

docs.title: State machine
docs.text:
┌─ refused (Team B refused)
                       │
        submit ─→ pending_values ─→ pending_verification ─→ approved ─→ executed
                       │                  │                    │
                       │                  └─ rejected          └─ failed
                       │                  
                       └─ expired (fill_ttl elapsed)
                       │
                       └─ cancelled (requester withdrew)
Status Meaning Who transitions it pending_values Waiting on Team B to fill Filler (POST /fill → pending_verification) or Refuser (POST /refuse → refused) or sweeper (TTL → expired) or requester (POST /cancel → cancelled) pending_verification Filled, waiting on source (and optionally security) approval Source approver via POST /verify (voted_as=source); security approver via POST /verify (voted_as=security) approved All required votes recorded; job enqueued JobService transitions it on agent's succeeded (→ executed) or failed (→ failed) executed Agent wrote the value to the destination provider Terminal failed Agent reported job failure Terminal refused Team B declined to provide the value Terminal, requester sees the refuse reason rejected Source or security approver rejected Terminal, requester sees the rejection reason cancelled Requester withdrew Terminal expired Fill window elapsed before Team B filled Terminal

Terminal states never transition. The N4 worker sweeper handles the expired path so the observable state catches up even when no fill attempt arrives.

docs.title: Separation of duties
docs.text:
The cross-team flow enforces a four-actor matrix. No single user can play more than one role on the same request. The API checks at every mutation:

requester  ≠  filler  ≠  source approver  ≠  security approver
Action Blocked when actor is also… POST /fill requester POST /verify (voted_as=source) requester or filler POST /verify (voted_as=security) requester or filler or the source approver on this same request

secret.security.approve is a global permission in v1, so a single user can carry both source and security capability. The SoD check catches the case where they try to cast both votes on the same request. The second attempt returns 403 with separation_of_duties_violated.

The SPA mirrors the API: the verify card hides the buttons the caller cannot use AND renders the reason ("You provided the values for this request.") so the operator knows they aren't broken. They're blocked by design.

docs.title: Permissions and seed roles
docs.text:
Two new permissions land with Slice N:

Permission Scope Description secret.value.provide Team-scoped (team_id in user_roles.scope) Holder appears in the inbox for that team and can fill cross-team requests targeting it. The sidebar Inbox entry only renders for users holding this permission at any scope. secret.security.approve Global in v1 Holder can cast the security vote on cross-team requests where the bound workflow has requires_security_approval=true. Per-project / per-environment scoping is deferred to a follow-up.

Two system roles ship as seed:

Role Permissions Notes value_provider secret.value.provide Assignment must carry a team_id in scope. The SPA's Assignments form enforces this with a "no team scope = global inbox access" type-to-confirm gate. security_approver secret.security.approve Used carefully, a holder can bypass the source-side workflow on cross-team requests. The Roles editor surfaces a type-to-confirm dialog the first time secret.security.approve is added to a role.

Both are is_system=true. The permission strings are editable, but the roles cannot be deleted. DELETE returns 409 system_row.

docs.title: Workflow knobs
docs.text:
workflow_definitions gets two new columns for cross-team semantics:

Column Default Use fill_ttl_seconds 86400 (24h) How long Team B has to fill before the sweeper expires the request requires_security_approval false When true, the bound request also needs a voted_as=security approve before transitioning to approved. PROD workflows typically flip this on.

The full min_approvers table for cross-team:

min_approvers Semantics Supported in v1 0 Auto-approve on fill, verify is a no-op ✓ 1 Single source approver required ✓ ≥ 2 Multi-approver source side No, SubmitCrossTeam returns 412 cross_team_min_approvers_unsupported

Multi-approver cross-team is deferred to v2 because it requires a distinct approvals counter on the request row vs the existing approvals table. Operators who need it today are blocked at submit; the error gives the SPA a clear toast.

docs.title: Workflow semantics frozen at submit
docs.text:
The bound workflow's requires_security_approval and min_approvers values are snapshotted onto the request row at submit time (snap_requires_security_approval + snap_min_approvers columns) so that a later workflow edit doesn't retroactively change in-flight semantics. The verify endpoint reads from the snapshot, not the live workflow row.

This is load-bearing: if you turn requires_security_approval=false to unblock an emergency, every request submitted after that change gets the new behaviour, but every request already in flight still needs the security vote it was submitted under. The audit log records both the live workflow ID and the snapshotted bools.

docs.title: Hard rules, what NEVER touches the value
docs.text: Surface Enforcement PostgreSQL columns access_requests carries no value columns; the agent's job consumes wraps via the same KMS-envelope path as the patch flow. The N1 schema CHECK constraints reject any cross-team row that's missing the target / destination / snapshot fields. Redis Used only for the inbox-count cache + idempotency tokens, no value cache. Logs The fill / refuse / verify handlers never log values, only key NAMES + actor identifiers. API responses The verify card response is value-free (no content_hash, no byte_length, no preview). The reveal session response is single-shot through the existing M-slice path. Browser state The SPA's fill page wipes the values from React state on submit success AND on component unmount. No localStorage / sessionStorage / IndexedDB writes anywhere in the flow. Audit metadata The audit log captures actor + key NAMES + workflow snapshot + correlation_id, never the value or any derivable canary.

docs.title: Worker sweepers
docs.text:
The cross-team-fill-window-expired sweeper closes the fill window for any pending_values request whose fill_expires_at has passed.

Knob Default Use SB_WORKER_CROSS_TEAM_FILL_EXPIRED_INTERVAL 30s How often the sweeper runs. 30s is the right cadence because fill_ttl_seconds is hours-scale by default.

The sweeper is defense in depth: the API's Fill check already rejects late writers with fill_window_expired. The sweeper ensures observable state (the inbox list, the request detail page, the metrics) catches up within 30s even when no fill attempt arrives to trigger that rejection.

Multi-replica safe, each worker takes a Redis lock on worker:sweeper:cross-team-fill-window-expired per tick. Lock contention is a metric, not a warning log.

docs.title: Reveal handling
docs.text:
Once a cross-team request lands in executed, the value is in the destination provider, but the requester typically wants to see the value once, in the SPA, to confirm the flow worked. That's exactly what the existing reveal session page handles (Slice M).

The Slice M4 page accepts both type='read' and (after Slice N3) type='cross_team' requests. The requester clicks "Reveal" from the request detail page; the SPA opens a single-shot bulk session; the page expires on TTL or on hide-now exactly like read flow.

The reveal session is bound to the requester, not the filler. The filler never sees the value after submitting it, they handed it off and the next time it appears, it's in the requester's provider.

docs.title: SPA surfaces
docs.text:
Surface Route Caller permission Submit drawer /projects/:id/env/:env_id (third CTA) secret.request Inbox list /inbox secret.value.provide (any scope, fail-closed sidebar) Fill / refuse /inbox/:request_id Same Verify card /requests/:id secret.approve (source) and/or secret.security.approve (security) Roles editor type-to-confirm /admin/roles role.edit Assignments team-pick gate /admin/assignments user_role.edit

Every cross-team mutation in the SPA invalidates both the request detail query and the inbox queries so the sidebar badge updates on the same tick the request transitions.

docs.title: Triage SQL
docs.text:
These queries assume psql against the API's Postgres.

Open inbox by team

SELECT id, requester_id, fill_expires_at, justification
FROM access_requests
WHERE type = 'cross_team'
  AND status = 'pending_values'
  AND target_team_id = $1
ORDER BY fill_expires_at;

Pending verification per project

SELECT id, requester_id, filled_by_user_id, filled_at, fill_comment
FROM access_requests
WHERE type = 'cross_team'
  AND status = 'pending_verification'
  AND source_project_id = $1
ORDER BY filled_at;

Expired in the last 24h (sweeper-flipped + service-layer-rejected)

SELECT id, requester_id, target_team_id, fill_expires_at, updated_at
FROM access_requests
WHERE type = 'cross_team'
  AND status = 'expired'
  AND updated_at > now() - interval '24 hours'
ORDER BY updated_at DESC;

Audit chain for one request, every transition surfaces with the shared correlation_id:

SELECT created_at, action, actor, metadata
FROM audit_events
WHERE correlation_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at;

docs.title: Error code reference
docs.text:
The API returns stable codes the SPA maps to friendly messages. Operators running curl smoke tests see the raw code in the response body.

Code Status Meaning out_of_scope_team 403 Caller doesn't cover this team's inbox out_of_scope_project 403 Caller doesn't have access to this project separation_of_duties_violated 403 Same actor tried to play two roles on one request cross_team_invalid_target 412 Target team / project / env chain doesn't resolve cross_team_destination_unbound 412 Destination provider connection isn't bound to the source project cross_team_keys_empty 412 destination_keys is empty cross_team_already_filled 409 Request is past pending_values fill_window_expired 410 TTL elapsed before fill cross_team_min_approvers_unsupported 412 Workflow min_approvers ≥ 2 is not supported in v1 cross_team_status_invalid_transition 409 Action doesn't apply to current status duplicate_vote 409 Caller already voted on this request

docs.title: Workflow resolution + scoped policy authoring
docs.text:
Cross-team requests resolve their workflow via the same PolicyEngine.Resolve(scope) path every other request type uses (secret.request / secret.read / cross_team). EPIC R (api#108) added a project-scoped applicability filter to the resolver:

  • A scoped policy_rules row authored by a section head via policy.author lives under a specific project_id and only participates in resolution when the request's scope carries that same project_id.
  • Platform global rules (project_id IS NULL) still apply universally. Platform's reserved priority band (>= 9000) wins over scoped overrides for the same selector, so a section head can't accidentally relax a cross-team approval requirement that platform pinned.

If you're authoring cross-team workflow rules at the project level, the same hard rules apply, scoped rules cannot match prod environments by construction. See Scoped policy authoring for the full operator model.

docs.title: Running locally with docker compose
docs.text:
A local loop for trying Secrets Bridge on one machine. The compose file lives in the api repo. It starts Postgres 17 and Redis 7, and can also build and run the api. The UI and the agent run from their own repos.

Local development only

This setup uses dev-only switches: SB_ENV=dev, the local KMS backend, and for the agent walkthrough SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_VAULT_ADDR and SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT. They are listed under Insecure switches. Never expose this stack beyond your machine and never load real secrets into it.

docs.title: 1. Start Postgres and Redis
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api.git
cd api
docker compose up -d postgres redis

docs.title: 2. Generate dev keys
docs.text:
Generate fresh keys for every new environment. Never reuse a value from these docs, an old compose file or another environment.

export SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"   # master key for the local KMS backend

The local KMS backend refuses to start without SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY.

docs.title: 3. Run the api
docs.text:
From the api checkout (Go 1.25 or newer):

export SB_ENV=dev   # allows the local KMS backend and seeds three dev users
export DATABASE_URL="postgres://secrets_bridge:devpass@localhost:5432/secrets_bridge?sslmode=disable"
export REDIS_URL="redis://localhost:6379/0"
go run ./cmd/api

In another terminal:

curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/readyz
# → {"status":"ready"}

On its first boot against an empty database the api seeds three dev users (an admin, an approver and a requester) and logs each user's email and password once. Copy them from that log output. Set SB_DEV_SEED_PASSWORD before the first boot if you want one shared password instead of a random one per user.

Running the api in a container instead

docker compose up -d --build also builds the api service from the repo's Dockerfile and runs it on port 8080. Export the keys from step 2 in the same shell first: the api container reads SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY from your environment and exits with an error when it is unset. Older copies of the compose file shipped a fixed dev master key instead; pull the latest main rather than reusing it.

docs.title: 4. Run the UI
docs.text:
From a checkout of the ui repo (Node 22 or newer):

npm ci
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:5173/. The Vite dev server proxies /api to http://localhost:8080. Sign in with the admin user from the api's boot log. SB_ENV=dev is what lets the session cookie work over plain http://localhost.

docs.title: Wiring an agent end to end (Vault example)
docs.text:
Agents onboard by enrollment: an admin creates a one-time token for a provider connection, and the agent exchanges it once for a persistent identity. The steps below run everything locally. See Agent onboarding for the model.

# 1. A throwaway Vault dev server on localhost, with a fake value in it.
export VAULT_DEV_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
docker run -d --name sb-vault-dev -p 127.0.0.1:8200:8200 \
  -e VAULT_DEV_ROOT_TOKEN_ID="$VAULT_DEV_TOKEN" hashicorp/vault:2.2
docker exec -e VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 -e VAULT_TOKEN="$VAULT_DEV_TOKEN" \
  sb-vault-dev vault kv put secret/team-alpha/dev/db DB_PASSWORD=not-a-real-password

# 2. Restart the api with SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_VAULT_ADDR=true (dev only):
#    the dev Vault listens on http://, which provider connections refuse
#    by default.

# 3. Sign in as the seeded admin. The password goes to jq on stdin, so
#    it never shows in the process list. The session cookie goes into a
#    private cookie jar; every call below sends it with -b.
CP=http://localhost:8080
JAR=$(mktemp) && chmod 600 "$JAR"
read -rp 'Admin email: ' SB_ADMIN_EMAIL
IFS= read -rsp 'Admin password: ' SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD; echo
printf '%s\n%s\n' "$SB_ADMIN_EMAIL" "$SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD" | jq -Rn '{email: input, password: input}' \
  | curl -fsS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/login" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @-

# 4. Register the Vault provider connection.
CONN_ID=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"local-vault","type":"vault","auth_method":"token","cluster_name":"local",
       "scope":{"address":"http://127.0.0.1:8200","mount":"secret"},
       "discover_interval_seconds":3600}' \
  | jq -r .id)

# 5. Create a one-time enrollment token for that connection (15 minutes by default).
SB_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections/$CONN_ID/agent-enrollment-token" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"local-agent","expected_cluster_name":"local","expected_provider_type":"vault"}' \
  | jq -j .enrollment_token)
export SB_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN

# 6. In the same shell, from a checkout of the agent repo: enroll on first
#    boot, then heartbeat. It runs in the background; `kill %1` stops it.
#    SB_VAULT_KV_MOUNT has to be the connection's mount from step 4. The
#    agent defaults to `kv`; with a mismatch it refuses discovery and
#    points reads and patches at the wrong mount.
cd ../agent   # wherever you cloned github.com/secrets-bridge/agent
mkdir -p .local
SB_CP_ENDPOINT="$CP" SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true \
SB_ENROLLMENT_ENABLED=true SB_IDENTITY_FILE="$PWD/.local/identity.json" \
SB_PROVIDER_TYPE=vault SB_CLUSTER_NAME=local \
SB_VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 SB_VAULT_TOKEN="$VAULT_DEV_TOKEN" \
SB_VAULT_KV_MOUNT=secret \
  go run ./cmd/agent > .local/agent.log 2>&1 &

# 7. After a few seconds the log shows "enrolled and persisted credential"
#    and the agent is listed, `active`, against the connection.
curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections/$CONN_ID/agents" | jq

The token is spent by step 6. The agent writes its identity to SB_IDENTITY_FILE (mode 0600) and reuses it on every restart, so a restart never needs a second token. To start over, revoke the agent, delete the identity file and create a new token.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Host port Service What 8080 api Control Plane API: /api/v1/*, /healthz, /readyz, /metrics. Change it with API_HOST_PORT when the api runs in compose. 5432 postgres Postgres 17 (secrets_bridge / devpass) 6379 redis Redis 7 4566 localstack (--profile awskms) LocalStack KMS, for trying the aws-kms backend 5173 Vite dev server The UI, from the ui repo 8200 Vault dev server Only if you started it for the agent walkthrough

The compose file publishes its ports on 127.0.0.1 only, so nothing is reachable from other machines. Older copies of the compose file published Postgres and Redis on every interface with fixed dev credentials; if yours still does, pull the latest main before you start it on a shared network.

docs.title: Resetting state
docs.text:
# Stop everything and drop the Postgres volume (wipes all data,
# including the seeded users)
docker compose down -v
docker rm -f sb-vault-dev   # if you started it
rm -f .local/identity.json  # in the agent checkout

docs.title: What docker compose is good for, what it's not
docs.text:
Use it for Don't use it for Local development Production Smoke tests and e2e in CI Multi-replica deployments Following along with this docs site Anything internet-exposed Demoing to a colleague Storing real secrets

For production, install the hardened Helm charts on a real Kubernetes cluster with managed Postgres and Redis and a real KMS backend. See Production deployment.

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
This page installs a Gateway for Release 1, which observes Argo CD only. You create a read-only Argo CD account, create the Gateway in the control plane, enroll it once from your workstation, install the chart, approve its connector, bind an Argo CD Application to a secret, and switch the environment's observation source to the Gateway.

Each control-plane step can be done in the console (Admin → Gateways) or with curl. Enrollment always runs from a shell, because the credential goes straight into a Kubernetes Secret.

Release 1 is in progress

Everything on this page is merged and has not passed QA. The control plane's own Argo CD poller (SB_GITOPS_ENABLED) still exists until the cutover in gateway#13 ships. An environment uses one observation source at a time, so a request gets Argo CD state from either the poller or the Gateway, never both.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Admin
    participant CP as Control plane
    participant Op as Operator workstation
    participant K8s as Your cluster
    participant GW as Gateway
    participant Argo as Argo CD
    Admin->>CP: POST /admin/gateways (fresh MFA)
    Admin->>CP: POST /admin/gateways/:id/enrollment-token
    CP-->>Admin: enrollment_token, shown once
    Admin->>Op: hand over the token
    Op->>CP: POST /gateways/enroll
    CP-->>Op: gateway_id and gateway_secret, shown once
    Op->>K8s: Secret with identity.json
    Op->>K8s: helm install secrets-bridge-gateway
    GW->>Argo: GET /api/v1/session/userinfo
    GW->>CP: heartbeat and catalog
    Admin->>CP: approve connector, create binding
    Admin->>CP: set the environment's observation source to gateway
    GW->>CP: claim task, post result

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The api from main, with migrations 0046 to 0048 applied. Migration 0047 adds gateway.mint, gateway.revoke, gateway.list and gateway.bind to the seed admin role. Migration 0048 adds the observation tables and each environment's observation source.
  • The worker from main, so the Gateway sweepers can be turned on (step 9).
  • An account that holds those permissions and has a second factor enrolled at /me/mfa. Every admin write on a Gateway needs a fresh second factor. The console asks for it when needed. For the curl path, the TOTP factor is the one you can complete from a shell.
  • kubectl, helm, jq, curl and the argocd CLI.
  • A namespace for the Gateway. The examples use tenant-a-uat.

docs.title: 1. Create a read-only Argo CD account
docs.text:
Add a local account with API key access and no login:

# argocd-cm
data:
  accounts.sb-gateway: apiKey

Give it applications, get on the AppProjects the Gateway may read, and nothing else:

# argocd-rbac-cm, one line per allowed AppProject
p, role:sb-gateway-read, applications, get, tenant-a-uat/*, allow
g, sb-gateway, role:sb-gateway-read

Do not add sync, override, action/*, update, delete, exec or logs, or anything on clusters, repositories, projects or accounts. The Gateway's transport already refuses every request except the two GETs it needs, but the token should not carry more than that either.

Generate a token and store it in a Secret without printing it:

argocd account generate-token --account sb-gateway --expires-in 2160h \
  | kubectl -n tenant-a-uat create secret generic sb-gateway-argocd-main \
      --from-file=token=/dev/stdin

The chart mounts the token as a file, and the Gateway re-reads it when it changes, so you can rotate it by updating the Secret.

docs.title: 2. Sign in and step up
docs.text:
The api uses a session cookie, so keep it in a private cookie jar. The password and the TOTP code are read from the terminal and passed to jq on stdin, so they never appear on a command line or in the process list.

CP=https://cp.example.com

JAR=$(mktemp) && chmod 600 "$JAR"
read -rp 'Admin email: ' SB_ADMIN_EMAIL
IFS= read -rsp 'Admin password: ' SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD; echo
printf '%s\n%s\n' "$SB_ADMIN_EMAIL" "$SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD" | jq -Rn '{email: input, password: input}' \
  | curl -fsS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/login" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @-
unset SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD

# Step up with your TOTP factor. The session stays MFA-fresh for 15 minutes.
FACTOR_ID=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/users/me/mfa/factors" \
  | jq -r 'map(select(.kind == "totp"))[0].id')
CHALLENGE_ID=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/mfa/challenge" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"kind":"totp"}' | jq -r .challenge_id)
IFS= read -rsp 'TOTP code: ' SB_TOTP_CODE; echo
printf '%s\n%s\n%s\n' "$CHALLENGE_ID" "$FACTOR_ID" "$SB_TOTP_CODE" \
  | jq -Rn '{challenge_id: input, factor_id: input, code: input}' \
  | curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -o /dev/null -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/mfa/verify" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @-
unset SB_TOTP_CODE

If a later write answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: step-up, the 15 minutes have passed. Run the step-up block again. See Authentication for the model.

In the console you skip this step: sign in, and the console runs the step-up dialog on the first write that needs it.

docs.title: 3. Create the Gateway and mint an enrollment token
docs.text:
In the console:

  1. Open Admin → Gateways (needs gateway.list) and select Create gateway.
  2. Fill in Name, Boundary and, if you want, Environment (optional), Max replicas and Max tasks in flight. Select Create gateway.
  3. The Create enrollment token panel opens next. Pick a Token lifetime (15 minutes, 1 hour or 24 hours) and, if you want, a Cluster name (optional), then select Create token. For a Gateway that is still pending you can also open it from the list and select Create enrollment token.
  4. The token is masked and shown once. Use Copy token, paste it at the silent prompt in step 4, and close the panel. The console keeps the token in memory only, and closing the panel clears the clipboard if it still holds the token.

With curl, create the Gateway record. name is a lower-case DNS-style label of up to 63 characters. boundary is a free label of up to 128 characters that says where the Gateway runs. environment_id is optional; when it is set, every binding for this Gateway must use that environment.

GW_ID=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateways" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"tenant-a-uat","boundary":"tenant-a-uat cluster"}' | jq -r .id)

The Gateway starts in status pending, with no credential. max_replicas (default 200) and max_inflight_tasks (default 20) can also be set here.

Mint a one-time enrollment token for it. The response carries the token once, so keep it out of your terminal output and your shell history:

SB_GATEWAY_ENROLL_TOKEN=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST \
    "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateways/$GW_ID/enrollment-token" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"expected_cluster_name":"tenant-a-uat","expires_in_seconds":900}' \
  | jq -r .enrollment_token)

Both fields are optional. expires_in_seconds defaults to 900 (15 minutes) and is clamped to 60 to 86400. When expected_cluster_name is set, enrollment must send the same cluster_name or it is refused. You can mint a token only while the Gateway is pending, and you can revoke an unused one with POST /api/v1/admin/gateway-enrollment-tokens/:id/revoke.

If someone else enrolls the Gateway, give them the token over a channel you would trust with a password. They read it at a silent prompt in step 4. Revoke an unused token from the Gateway's Enrollment tokens list in the console, or with the route above.

docs.title: 4. Enroll and store the identity
docs.text:
The pod never enrolls. You exchange the token for the Gateway credential once, from your workstation, and write the result straight into a Secret. The token and the secret never appear on a command line, in shell history or on disk.

# Skip this read if you minted the token in this shell in step 3.
IFS= read -rsp 'Enrollment token: ' SB_GATEWAY_ENROLL_TOKEN; echo

printf '%s' "$SB_GATEWAY_ENROLL_TOKEN" \
  | jq -Rs '{enrollment_token: ., cluster_name: "tenant-a-uat"}' \
  | curl -fsS -X POST "$CP/api/v1/gateways/enroll" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @- \
  | jq -ce '{gateway_id, gateway_secret}' \
  | kubectl -n tenant-a-uat create secret generic sb-gateway-identity \
      --from-file=identity.json=/dev/stdin
unset SB_GATEWAY_ENROLL_TOKEN

printf is a shell builtin, so the token does not show up in the process list. The enrollment endpoint answers 201 with gateway_id and gateway_secret, and the Gateway turns active.

The token is single use. If any step of the pipeline fails after the control plane answered, the credential is lost: revoke the Gateway and create a new one. Enrollment errors are closed codes:

Status Code Meaning 401 enrollment_token_invalid, enrollment_token_expired Unknown or expired token. Mint a new one 403 enrollment_token_revoked The token was revoked 403 https_required The request did not reach the api over TLS. Enrollment is refused over plain http outside SB_ENV=dev 409 enrollment_token_already_consumed, gateway_already_enrolled The token or the Gateway was used already 400 cluster_name_mismatch cluster_name differs from the token's expected_cluster_name

If your Secrets come from a vault through External Secrets Operator, store the same JSON in the vault and render it into a Secret under the key identity.json.

docs.title: 5. Install the chart
docs.text:
Pin the image by digest. Check its signature first, as described in Verifying images and charts. NetworkPolicy cannot match hostnames, so list the CIDRs that the control plane and Argo CD resolve to.

# gateway-values.yaml
image:
  digest: sha256:<gateway-digest>
cp:
  endpoint: https://cp.example.com
  egress:
    cidrs: [192.0.2.10/32]
identity:
  existingSecret: sb-gateway-identity
connectors:
  argocd:
    - name: argocd-main               # the connector id the control plane sees
      baseURL: https://argocd.example.com
      tokenSecret:
        name: sb-gateway-argocd-main
        key: token
      allowedProjects: [tenant-a-uat]
      applications:
        - id: payments-api            # the target id you bind in step 7
          name: payments-api          # the Argo CD Application
      egress:
        cidrs: [198.51.100.20/32]
        port: 443

helm install secrets-bridge-gateway \
  oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-gateway \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --namespace tenant-a-uat -f gateway-values.yaml

The chart renders a Deployment (2 replicas sharing one identity), a ConfigMap with the connectors file, a ServiceAccount with no Role and no mounted token, a NetworkPolicy with no ingress and egress only to DNS, the control plane and each Argo CD endpoint, and a PodDisruptionBudget. It renders no Secret, Role, Service, Ingress or volume claim. helm install fails with a message naming the value when the image is not pinned, cp.endpoint is not https://, the identity Secret is not named, a connector is incomplete, or a NetworkPolicy peer is missing.

For an Argo CD in the same cluster, use selectors instead of CIDRs, and the full list of values, see the chart README.

docs.title: 6. Verify
docs.text:
Wait for the pods to turn ready. Readiness runs gateway healthcheck inside the container, and it passes only after the control plane has accepted a heartbeat and the catalog and the Argo CD token check has passed.

kubectl -n tenant-a-uat rollout status deploy/secrets-bridge-gateway
kubectl -n tenant-a-uat exec deploy/secrets-bridge-gateway -- \
  /usr/local/bin/gateway healthcheck
kubectl -n tenant-a-uat logs deploy/secrets-bridge-gateway

In the log, look for identity loaded and connectors bound.

Then check the control plane. In the console, Admin → Gateways shows the status, replicas and last heartbeat in UTC. Select the Gateway's name to see its replicas and Advertised connectors. With curl, GET /api/v1/admin/gateways needs gateway.list and no step-up:

curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateways" \
  | jq '.items[] | {id, name, status, last_seen_at, replicas_seen, catalog_version}'

curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateways/$GW_ID" \
  | jq '{replicas: [.replicas[] | {replica_id, status, last_seen_at}],
         connectors: [.connectors[] | {id, connector_id, kind, status, targets}]}'

The Gateway shows status: "active", each replica appears with a recent last_seen_at, and the connector argocd-main is listed with status advertised and the target payments-api.

Until a task is queued for it, each claim answers 204 and the Gateway backs off up to once every 30 seconds (SB_GATEWAY_CLAIM_IDLE_MAX). That is normal and does not affect readiness.

docs.title: 7. Approve the connector and bind a target
docs.text:
Advertising a connector approves nothing. An admin with gateway.bind approves it and binds a target.

In the console, open the Gateway from Admin → Gateways:

  1. Under Advertised connectors, select Approve… next to argocd-main, then Approve connector. Approving grants the Gateway nothing in Argo CD.
  2. Select Bind a target. Choose the Argo CD target, the Project and Environment, and a Secret scope: either A catalog secret bound to the project (then Secret) or A provider connection and a secret path (then Provider connection and Secret path).
  3. Pick an Observation deadline (15 minutes to 6 hours, 30 minutes by default) and select Create binding.

The binding appears under Bindings, where Delete… removes it.

With curl, approve the connector using its id (a UUID) from the detail call above:

CONNECTOR_ID=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateways/$GW_ID" \
  | jq -r '.connectors[] | select(.connector_id == "argocd-main") | .id')

curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST \
  "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateways/$GW_ID/connectors/$CONNECTOR_ID/approve" | jq '{connector_id, status}'

Then bind one advertised Argo CD target to a secret scope in an environment. A binding names the Gateway, the environment, either a secret_id (a secret bound to the environment's project) or a provider_connection_id with a secret_ref, and the Argo CD connector and target:

curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateway-bindings" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"gateway_id\":\"$GW_ID\",
       \"environment_id\":\"<environment-id>\",
       \"secret_id\":\"<secret-id>\",
       \"argocd_connector_id\":\"$CONNECTOR_ID\",
       \"argocd_target_id\":\"payments-api\",
       \"observation_timeout_seconds\":1800}" | jq

observation_timeout_seconds defaults to 1800 and must be 60 to 86400. Release 1 bindings expect the single stage argocd_context. The api refuses a binding with a closed code, for example connector_not_approved, target_not_advertised, target_stale (the Gateway no longer advertises it), environment_outside_gateway, secret_not_in_project or binding_exists. GET /api/v1/admin/gateway-bindings?gateway_id=<id> lists bindings and DELETE /api/v1/admin/gateway-bindings/:id removes one, and cancels its open tasks with the reason binding_removed.

docs.title: 8. Switch the environment to Gateway observation
docs.text:
A binding alone creates no tasks. Each environment has an observation source, and only an environment set to gateway gets Gateway tasks:

Source What observes a change executed in the environment control_plane (default) The control plane's own Argo CD poller, when SB_GITOPS_ENABLED and SB_WORKER_GITOPS_ENABLED are on. Otherwise nothing gateway The Gateways bound to the environment. The control-plane poller is skipped for these requests none Nothing

The source is read once when a request reaches executed, so a request is observed by one of them, never both. Switching away from gateway cancels the environment's open Gateway tasks with the reason source_changed. The requests themselves are not affected.

In the console (needs gateway.bind), open Admin → Projects, select the project, and find the environment on the Environments tab. The Observation column shows the current source. Select Change…, choose Gateway in the Observation for dialog, and select Save.

With curl, the route needs gateway.bind and a fresh second factor (step 2). The body holds no secret, so it can go on the command line:

ENV_ID=<environment-id>

curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/admin/environments/$ENV_ID/observation-source" | jq

curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X PUT "$CP/api/v1/admin/environments/$ENV_ID/observation-source" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"observation_source":"gateway"}' \
  | jq '{observation_source, previous_observation_source, tasks_cancelled}'

A value other than control_plane, gateway or none answers 400 invalid_observation_source, and an unknown environment 404 environment_not_found. The change is audited as environment.observation_source.update.

docs.title: 9. Turn on the worker sweepers
docs.text:
The worker runs four Gateway sweepers when SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED is true (default false):

  • observation-leases puts tasks whose lease ran out back in the queue.
  • observation-deadlines closes open tasks past their deadline as timed_out, with the reason gateway_unavailable or deadline_reached.
  • gateways-stale moves a Gateway from active to stale after SB_WORKER_GATEWAYS_STALE_AFTER (default 2m) without a heartbeat. The next accepted heartbeat moves it back to active.
  • gateway-replicas-prune deletes replica rows not seen within SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_REPLICAS_RETENTION (default 24h).

The intervals and floors are in the configuration reference. Without the sweepers, a claim still takes over an expired lease, and reading a request's observations closes that request's overdue tasks. Tasks of requests nobody opens stay open past their deadline, and Gateways never turn stale.

docs.title: 10. Check a request
docs.text:
Submit and approve a change to the bound secret in that environment. When the agent has written it and the request is executed, the request page shows a panel titled Argo CD (observed by Gateway tenant-a-uat), marked Observed operational state · times in UTC. It shows:

  • The rollup: Pending, Unverified, Timed out or, when no binding covers the change, No observation configured. None of these is a failure of the request. The panel refreshes every 20 seconds while the rollup is pending, and when the window regains focus.
  • For each task, the Gateway, the verdict, the task state and its deadline or closing time, and the reason in words, for example "Only Argo CD context was observed. Argo CD health and sync are operational state, never proof that the new value reached the app."
  • For the Argo CD stage, the outcome (Observed or Not observed), the observed time, the Sync, Health, Last operation, Revision, Operation finished and Reconciled facts, and the caveat "Argo CD reports Healthy and Synced. This is the operational state, not proof the new value reached the app." Evidence details lists the connector, target, confidence, linkage, Gateway, replica and attempt ids.

The same data comes from GET /api/v1/requests/<id>/observations, behind the same read check as the request itself:

curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/requests/<request-id>/observations" \
  | jq '{observation_source, rollup, label,
         tasks: [.tasks[] | {gateway_name, state, verdict, verdict_reason,
                             stages: [.stages[] | {stage, outcome, observed_at, caveats, facts}]}]}'

On the Gateway's detail panel, Recent tasks lists the latest 25 tasks with their state, verdict and attempts. With curl, GET /api/v1/admin/gateways/$GW_ID/tasks (needs gateway.list) takes ?state= and ?limit= (1 to 500, default 100).

docs.title: Disable, enable or revoke a Gateway
docs.text:
Disabling is reversible. A disabled Gateway's calls are refused with 401, its leased tasks go back to the queue, and their old attempts can no longer post a result. It keeps its credential, and enabling it returns it to active (or pending if it never enrolled). In the console, open the Gateway and select Disable… or Enable…. With curl (needs gateway.revoke and a fresh second factor):

curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X PUT "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateways/$GW_ID/enabled" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"enabled":false}' | jq '{status}'

A revoked Gateway answers 409 gateway_revoked.

Revoking is final. In the console, select Revoke…, or:

# Needs gateway.revoke and a fresh second factor.
curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/admin/gateways/$GW_ID/revoke" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"reason":"decommissioned"}' | jq '{status, revoked_at}'

reason is optional, a lower-case code of up to 64 characters. The next heartbeat, catalog upload or task call gets 401, and leased tasks go back to the queue. A task belongs to one Gateway, so its open tasks end timed_out with the reason gateway_unavailable at their deadline. The pods stay up and not ready with the reason in their logs. There is no credential rotation in Release 1: to replace a credential, revoke the Gateway, create a new one, enroll it and update the identity Secret.

See Troubleshooting when something does not turn ready.

docs.title: Sign in with Google
docs.text:
An admin can connect the company's Google Workspace from the console, with no environment variables and no redeploy. People in the allowed Workspace domains then sign in with Google. By default, the first sign-in creates an account that waits until an admin approves it and gives it a role.

Merged, not yet through QA

Google sign-in is in the api, console and worker on main, but it has not passed a QA cycle. See Product status.

This page covers:

  • setting it up: the public address, the Google OAuth client, the console settings, Test and Turn on;
  • who can sign in and how accounts are matched;
  • approving new accounts, and the option to skip approval;
  • connecting Google to an existing account;
  • the worker message for new accounts;
  • how it sits next to the env-var OIDC provider and the break-glass admin.

The examples use https://secrets.example.com as the install's address and example.com as the Workspace domain.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor P as New user
    participant UI as Console
    participant API as api
    participant G as Google
    actor A as Admin
    P->>UI: Sign in with Google
    UI->>API: GET /api/v1/auth/sso/google/start
    API->>G: redirect with PKCE, nonce and state
    G->>API: GET /api/v1/auth/sso/google/callback?code=...
    API->>API: check email_verified, hd and email domain
    API->>API: create account, waiting for approval
    API->>UI: session cookie, redirect
    UI->>P: Waiting for approval page
    A->>UI: Admin → Users, Approve with a role and scope
    UI->>API: POST /api/v1/users/:id/approve
    P->>UI: Check again
    UI->>P: console with the granted access

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • an account with a global auth.sso.edit grant and an enrolled second factor. The seeded admin role holds auth.sso.edit, so the bootstrap admin can do this right after the first sign-in;
  • a public https address for the install, the one people type in the browser;
  • a Google Workspace and a Google Cloud project in it where you can create OAuth clients.

Every change asks for a fresh second factor. Saving the public address or the waiting limit, creating, editing or removing Google, replacing the client secret, Test, Turn on and Turn off all go through the step-up dialog (RequireFreshMFA). Whoever holds auth.sso.edit decides who can sign in, and the step-up means a stolen session cookie alone can't change these settings.

docs.title: 1. Set the public address
docs.text:
Redirect URIs are built from the install's configured public address, never from the request's Host or X-Forwarded-* headers. A forged header can't send the authorization code somewhere else. The address comes from one of two places:

Source How In the console SB_PUBLIC_URL Set it in the api's environment, for example in the chart's secrets.existingSecret. The worker reads the same Secret. Shown read-only, with "Set by SB_PUBLIC_URL on this install" The console Admin → Sign-in → Public address. The field is prefilled from the address you are using. Editable

When SB_PUBLIC_URL is set it always wins, and PUT /sso/settings refuses to change the address (409 public_url_from_env).

The address must be an absolute https URL with no user info, query or fragment. A trailing slash is dropped. Plain http is accepted only for localhost or a loopback address, and only when SB_ENV=dev. The api refuses to start with an invalid SB_PUBLIC_URL. The console warns, without blocking, when a saved address isn't https or looks internal.

Google can't be turned on until an address is set, and while none is set the login page doesn't offer Google.

The Public address card also holds the waiting limit, the most accounts that can wait for approval at once. It defaults to 50 and accepts 1 to 10,000. See The waiting limit.

docs.title: 2. Create the OAuth client in Google Cloud Console
docs.text:
With the address saved, Admin → Sign-in → Google → Set up Google shows the redirect URL to copy. It is always the public address plus /api/v1/auth/sso/google/callback:

https://secrets.example.com/api/v1/auth/sso/google/callback

In the Google Cloud project:

  1. Set the OAuth consent screen's user type to Internal, so only accounts in your Workspace can use the client.
  2. Create an OAuth client ID of application type Web application.
  3. Add the redirect URL above under Authorized redirect URIs, exactly as the console shows it.
  4. Copy the client ID and the client secret.

Secrets Bridge uses Google's fixed issuer (https://accounts.google.com) and its discovery document, so you don't enter an issuer. It asks for the openid, email and profile scopes.

docs.title: 3. Enter the client in the console
docs.text:
In the Set up Google drawer:

Field What to enter Client ID From the OAuth client. Required, at most 255 characters, no spaces. Client secret From the OAuth client. Saved encrypted and never shown again. Workspace domains One per line, for example example.com. At least one, at most 20. They are lowercased and de-duplicated. New people Wait for approval (the default) or Let them in right away. Role for new people Only with Let them in right away. Optional. See Letting people in without approval.

The provider is saved turned off.

The client secret is write-only. It is envelope-encrypted with the configured KMS (a fresh data key, AES-256-GCM), the same way TOTP secrets are stored. No response returns it, only client_secret_set: true, and it is never logged or put in audit metadata. The console shows it as "Saved", with Replace… to set a new one. Replacing it is its own call, PUT /sso/providers/:id/secret, audited as sso_provider.secret_rotate. PUT /sso/providers/:id refuses a client_secret field with 400.

docs.title: 4. Test, then turn it on
docs.text:
Test sends you through Google with your own account and back to Admin → Sign-in. It runs every check a real sign-in runs, creates nothing, issues no session, and works while Google is still off. The result shows as "Google sign-in works." or as the reason it didn't pass, and only the admin who ran it sees that reason.

Turn on needs a public address, a client secret and at least one domain. If any is missing the api answers 409 provider_not_ready with a missing list, and the console names what to set. Once on, the login page shows Sign in with Google above the password form.

Changes take effect on the next sign-in, without a restart: the OAuth client is built from the saved settings on every round trip.

docs.title: Who can sign in
docs.text:
On every Google sign-in, including returning users, the api checks:

  • the email is verified by Google (email_verified);
  • the ID token's hd claim (the Workspace domain) is present and in the allowed domains;
  • the email's domain is in the allowed domains as well.

hd is only present for Workspace accounts. A personal Google account with an address in an allowed domain has no hd, so it is refused. Removing a domain from the list refuses people in it from their next sign-in. When exactly one domain is allowed, the api also passes it to Google as the hd hint, so the account chooser offers only accounts in that Workspace.

Accounts are matched by Google's issuer and subject, never by email. The binding lives in the user_identities table, unique on (issuer, subject). The first sign-in of a Google identity:

  • creates a new account when its email isn't used by any account here;
  • is refused when the email already belongs to an account. That person signs in with their password and connects Google instead. This stops a Google account with, say, the bootstrap admin's address from reaching the bootstrap admin's account.

The round trip itself uses PKCE (S256), a nonce and a single-use state that lives 5 minutes and is bound to the browser by the sb_sso_state cookie. Return paths must be on the same origin, as for the env-var OIDC provider.

Every refused sign-in gets the same answer. The browser goes to /login?error=sso, and the login page says "You couldn't be signed in with that account." whatever the reason. The page never tells an outsider which emails have accounts. The reason goes to the audit log; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Approve new accounts
docs.text:
With Wait for approval on, a new account starts waiting. Until it is approved it can only read GET /users/me and sign out. Every other route answers 403 account_pending_approval, and the console sends the person to a Waiting for approval page with Check again and Sign out. This is enforced at session validation and at sign-in. If a waiting account signs in through the env-var OIDC provider, its group mapping is skipped, so it gets no role from IdP groups either.

Admins who can approve see:

  • a count on Users in the sidebar;
  • a banner on Overview with a link while anyone is waiting;
  • the Waiting for approval list on Admin → Users, longest wait first;
  • optionally, a webhook message from the worker.

Approving and declining need a global user_role.edit. A team-scoped grant, or team.edit, is not enough.

Approve… picks a role and, optionally, limits it to a team or a project. The api grants the role and clears the waiting flag in one transaction, so a failed grant leaves the account waiting. The scope is checked with the same rules as POST /user-roles: only project_id, team_id, environment, secret_ref_prefix and provider_type are accepted, each a non-empty string, IDs as UUIDs. A malformed scope is refused with 400 instead of being widened. The person gets the access on their next request, or after Check again.

Decline… disables a waiting account after a confirmation, and its sessions end on their next use. Decline only works on waiting accounts (409 user_not_pending otherwise), so it can't disable an active account or the break-glass admin. A declined account keeps its waiting flag, so it can't be approved or re-enabled from the console, and that Google account can't sign in again.

docs.title: The waiting limit
docs.text: At most 50 accounts can wait at once by default; change the limit on Admin → Sign-in → Public address. Past it, new Google sign-ins are refused with the same generic page until you approve or decline some. Declined accounts don't count. Refusals at the limit are audited as user.pending_refused, aggregated per 10-minute window: the first refusal in a window writes one event, and the next window writes a summary with the count and the first and last times. A burst of sign-ins can't fill the append-only audit log.

docs.title: Letting people in without approval
docs.text:
With Let them in right away, a new account starts active. You can pick a Role for new people, granted globally when the account is created. Without one, the account starts with no role, and an admin grants one on the Users page.

The default role must be non-privileged: every permission it holds must be in secret.list, secret.request and audit.read (audit.read only shows a user their own events). The api refuses anything else with 400 default_role_privileged, and a default role with approval on with 400 default_role_needs_approval_off. The seeded developer role doesn't qualify, because it holds secret.reveal.direct. Create a role with only those permissions if you want approval off.

The rule holds after the provider is saved too:

  • widening a role that a provider uses as its default (PUT /roles/:id/permissions) is refused with 409 role_is_sso_default, and deleting it with 409 until you choose another default;
  • the role is checked again at every sign-in. If it no longer qualifies, the new account waits for approval like any other, and the api audits sso_provider.default_role_refused.

docs.title: Connect Google to an existing account
docs.text:
Existing accounts, including the bootstrap admin, are never linked by email. The owner connects Google from their profile:

  1. Sign in with the password.
  2. Open the profile page and click Connect Google. It asks for a fresh second factor.
  3. Choose the Google account. It must pass the same checks as a sign-in.
  4. Back in the console, the profile shows the connected account.

Google must be turned on. The round trip is bound to the session that started it: the callback parks the result in a one-time ticket that lives 2 minutes, and the console redeems it with POST /auth/sso/google/finish, which only succeeds on that same session (otherwise 403 sso_ticket_refused). A Google identity already connected to another account is refused (409 link_refused, reason identity_taken), and the profile says so. A link is audited as user.identity_link.

Disconnect… also needs a fresh second factor and is audited as user.identity_unlink. After it, the owner signs in with their password again.

An account created by a Google sign-in can't disconnect Google. It was given a random password nobody knows, so Google is its only way in. DELETE /users/me/identities/google answers 409 identity_required, and the profile explains why instead of offering Disconnect….

docs.title: Notify admins from the worker
docs.text:
The worker's users-pending sweeper posts a message when accounts start waiting. It needs SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_URL, and isn't registered without it; the console's count and banner still work.

Variable Default Notes SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_URL (unset) Where to post. Required for this message. SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_SLACK_FORMAT false true posts {"text": ...} for a Slack incoming webhook. SB_WORKER_USERS_PENDING_INTERVAL 1m How often it runs, and so the most often admins hear about new accounts. At least 30s, or the worker refuses to start. SB_PUBLIC_URL (unset) Used for the link to Admin → Users. Unset, the address saved in the console is used.

Each run posts at most one message. It covers the accounts that started waiting since the last message: up to 10 by email, oldest first, then "and N more", the total still waiting when older ones are left, and a link to <public address>/admin/users:

[info] 2 new accounts are waiting for approval
• sara@example.com
• omar@example.com
Approve or decline them in Admin → Users: https://secrets.example.com/admin/users

The message carries emails only, never display names, because a display name comes from the person's Google account and can contain anything. It goes to the webhook only. The worker logs counts, never who is waiting. Each account is announced once. A failed post is retried on the next run, together with anyone who arrived since. Declined accounts are left out.

docs.title: Next to the env-var OIDC provider
docs.text:
The env-var OIDC provider (SB_OIDC_ISSUER and the other SB_OIDC_* variables) keeps working as before. When both are configured, the login page shows two buttons, Sign in with Google and Sign in with single sign-on, and each provider handles its own sign-ins. The env-var provider still matches accounts by verified email and doesn't create waiting accounts.

When SB_OIDC_ISSUER is already Google (https://accounts.google.com), the console refuses to add Google (409 env_provider_is_google), the login page doesn't offer the console provider, and a provider saved earlier can't be turned on.

Password sign-in and the break-glass admin are never turned off by these settings. No sign-in setting disables POST /auth/login, and decline only touches waiting accounts. If Google is misconfigured or down, sign in with the bootstrap admin's password and fix it under Admin → Sign-in.

docs.title: Audit events
docs.text:
Action When sso_provider.create, .update, .delete, .enable, .disable Google changed in the console. Old and new values of the domains, the approval setting and the default role. Never the secret, only whether one is set. sso_provider.secret_rotate The client secret replaced sso_settings.update The public address or the waiting limit changed, with old and new values sso_provider.test A Test round trip, success or denied with error_kind auth.sso.callback A Google sign-in or Connect Google round trip, success or denied with error_kind user.pending An account created waiting for approval user.sso_provision An account created active, with approval off user.approve, user_role.grant An admin approved an account, with the role and scope user.decline An admin declined an account user.pending_refused Sign-ins refused at the waiting limit, aggregated per 10 minutes sso_provider.default_role_refused A default role no longer qualified at sign-in, so the account waits user.identity_link, user.identity_unlink Google connected to or disconnected from an account

None of them carries a token, code, ticket or secret.

docs.title: API
docs.text: The routes are listed in the HTTP API reference, and the permissions in the permissions catalog.

docs.title: Object storage
docs.text:
The api can keep media files in an S3 bucket or on any server that speaks the S3 API, such as MinIO. Postgres keeps only the metadata for each file.

In progress

Object storage is implemented in api#255 and the chart values in charts#40 and charts#42. It has not passed QA yet. See Product status.

docs.title: What is stored there
docs.text:
Only media. Today that means the project and team logos served by GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/logo and GET /api/v1/teams/{id}/logo. New media fields added later use the same store.

Never stored in object storage:

  • secret values, wrapped or unwrapped;
  • tokens, credentials or wrap bodies;
  • audit records. Audit events for logo changes record metadata only (sha256, byte length, dimensions), never image bytes or URLs.

docs.title: Object keys
docs.text:
Each object is keyed by the sha256 of its content:

<prefix>/logos/<kind>/<entity-id>/<sha256>.png
Part Value <prefix> SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX <kind> project or team (singular, lower case) <entity-id> The project or team id <sha256> Hash of the re-encoded PNG. It is also the ETag the api returns.

For example, with SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX=secrets-bridge a project logo lives at secrets-bridge/logos/project/<project-id>/<sha256>.png. Without a prefix the key starts at logos/. The api trims slashes at either end of the prefix.

Uploading the same image twice maps to the same key, so writes are idempotent. When a logo is replaced, the api deletes the old object after the database row points at the new one. The row stores the full key, so changing SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX later does not move existing logos: they stay at their old keys.

docs.title: How a logo moves through the system
docs.text:
The bucket stays private. The console never talks to it. Every read and write goes through the api, so the existing authorization rules apply: reading a project logo needs read scope on that project, a team logo has the same visibility as the team, and uploading or removing a logo needs the global team.edit permission.

sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as Console
    participant API as api
    participant OS as Object store
    participant PG as Postgres
    UI->>API: PUT /api/v1/projects/id/logo (PNG or JPEG)
    API->>API: Validate and re-encode to PNG, compute sha256
    API->>OS: PutObject at prefix/logos/kind/id/sha256.png
    API->>PG: Upsert metadata row (object key, sha256, size)
    API->>OS: Delete previous object, if any
    API-->>UI: 200 with logo_version
    UI->>API: GET /api/v1/projects/id/logo
    API->>PG: Read metadata row
    API->>OS: GetObject
    API-->>UI: image/png with ETag

If the object write fails, the database row is not changed and the api returns 503 logo storage is unavailable. If the row write fails, the api removes the object it just wrote, unless the current row already uses that same key, and returns 500 internal error. If deleting the old object fails, the object is left behind and the api logs a warning; no row points at it.

On reads, the api answers If-None-Match from the row without reading the object. A row that still holds its image in the png column (before the backfill, or written by an old replica during a rollout) is served from those bytes with the same headers and ETag. If a row points at an object that is missing, the api returns 404 and logs an error that names the key; the key is not in the response body.

The api never sets an ACL on an object and does not issue presigned URLs.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The api reads these environment variables. The full list is in the Configuration reference.

Env var Notes Env var Default --- --- SB_OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET unset SB_OBJECTSTORE_REGION unset SB_OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT unset SB_OBJECTSTORE_FORCE_PATH_STYLE false SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX unset SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE unset SB_OBJECTSTORE_KMS_KEY_ID unset SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL true

Credentials come from the standard AWS SDK chain: IRSA, an instance role, or AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in the environment. This is the same chain the aws-kms backend uses. There are no SB_OBJECTSTORE_* variables for credentials.

docs.title: Boot behaviour
docs.text:
State What the api does Not configured (no SB_OBJECTSTORE_* set) Boots normally. PUT and DELETE on a logo return 503 logo storage is not configured. Logos still stored in Postgres keep being served. The api never falls back to writing media to Postgres. If inline logos exist, the boot logs a warning with their count. Misconfigured Refuses to boot with an error. This covers any SB_OBJECTSTORE_* setting without a bucket, a bucket without a region, an unknown SSE value, aws:kms without a key id, a key id with another SSE mode, a malformed endpoint or prefix, a plain http:// endpoint when SB_ENV is not dev, and a SB_OBJECTSTORE_FORCE_PATH_STYLE that is not true or false. Configured, bucket unreachable Refuses to boot. The api calls HeadBucket at start and gives up after 15 seconds. A denied HeadBucket (see the IAM policy) fails the same way. Configured and reachable Logs object storage ready, writes and reads logos in the bucket, and starts the backfill unless SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL=false.

When the bucket is reachable at boot but fails later, logo requests that need it return 503 logo storage is unavailable. The rest of the api keeps working.

docs.title: Helm chart values
docs.text:
The secrets-bridge chart maps objectStore.* values to the SB_OBJECTSTORE_* variables on the api:

Value Default Env var on the api objectStore.enabled false Turns the settings below on. Off renders no SB_OBJECTSTORE_* at all. objectStore.bucket "" SB_OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET (required when enabled) objectStore.region "" SB_OBJECTSTORE_REGION (required when enabled) objectStore.endpoint "" SB_OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT objectStore.prefix "" SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX objectStore.sse AES256 SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE. "" renders no variable, so no SSE header is sent. objectStore.kmsKeyId "" SB_OBJECTSTORE_KMS_KEY_ID (only with sse: aws:kms) objectStore.forcePathStyle false SB_OBJECTSTORE_FORCE_PATH_STYLE, always rendered as "true" or "false" objectStore.logoBackfill true SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL, always rendered as "true" or "false" objectStore.credentials.existingSecret "" Name of a Secret with static keys. When set, the api gets AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY through secretKeyRef. objectStore.credentials.accessKeyIdKey AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID Key in that Secret for the access key id objectStore.credentials.secretAccessKeyKey AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY Key in that Secret for the secret access key api.networkPolicy.egress.objectStore.enabled true Adds a TCP egress rule to the object store when objectStore.enabled api.networkPolicy.egress.objectStore.to [] NetworkPolicy peers that narrow the rule. Empty allows the port to any destination.

The chart's default for sse is AES256, while the api on its own sends no SSE header when SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE is unset. Only the api gets these variables; the worker does not read media.

The chart does not take credentials in values. On AWS, use IRSA through api.serviceAccount.annotations. For an S3-compatible server, use objectStore.credentials.existingSecret. Static keys cannot be combined with kms.backend=aws-kms, because the SDK prefers them over IRSA and the KMS client would sign with them.

The chart refuses to render when object storage is enabled and bucket or region is empty, sse is not AES256, aws:kms or empty, sse: aws:kms has no kmsKeyId, kmsKeyId is set with another sse, the endpoint is not http(s)://host[:port], the endpoint is plain http:// with env=production, the prefix has an empty, . or .. segment, logoBackfill is not true or false, or static keys are combined with kms.backend=aws-kms.

The egress port comes from objectStore.endpoint: its explicit port, else 443 for https and 80 for http, and 443 when no endpoint is set (AWS S3). To manage the rule yourself, set api.networkPolicy.egress.objectStore.enabled: false and add it to api.networkPolicy.egress.extraRules.

docs.title: AWS S3 with IRSA
docs.text:
1. Create a bucket, for example example-bucket, in the same region as the cluster. Keep the defaults for Object Ownership (ACLs disabled) and Block Public Access (all four settings on).
  2. Turn on default encryption. See Encryption at rest.
  3. Create an IAM role for the api ServiceAccount with a trust policy for your cluster's OIDC provider, and attach the least-privilege policy below.
  4. Annotate the api ServiceAccount and set the values:
api:
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/secrets-bridge-api
objectStore:
  enabled: true
  bucket: example-bucket
  region: us-east-1
  prefix: secrets-bridge
  sse: aws:kms
  kmsKeyId: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000

If the api role already has access for the aws-kms backend, you can add the S3 policy to the same role.

To keep S3 traffic inside the VPC, add an S3 gateway endpoint to the cluster's route tables. The api needs no extra setting for a gateway endpoint.

docs.title: S3-compatible servers (MinIO)
docs.text:
For MinIO or another S3 API, set the endpoint and turn on path-style addressing. Static credentials come from an existing Secret, never from values.

Read the keys at silent prompts (paste each, then Enter) so they never reach a command line, the shell history or the process list. This works in bash and zsh:

read -rs SB_S3_KEY_ID
read -rs SB_S3_SECRET
kubectl -n secrets-bridge create secret generic secrets-bridge-objectstore \
  --from-file=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<(printf '%s' "$SB_S3_KEY_ID") \
  --from-file=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<(printf '%s' "$SB_S3_SECRET")
unset SB_S3_KEY_ID SB_S3_SECRET

objectStore:
  enabled: true
  endpoint: https://s3.example.com
  forcePathStyle: true
  bucket: example-bucket
  region: us-east-1
  prefix: secrets-bridge
  sse: ""                  # no SSE header; see the notes below
  credentials:
    existingSecret: secrets-bridge-objectstore
api:
  networkPolicy:
    egress:
      objectStore:
        to:
          - namespaceSelector:
              matchLabels:
                kubernetes.io/metadata.name: minio

The keys in the Secret above match the default credentials.accessKeyIdKey and credentials.secretAccessKeyKey, so those don't need to be set. Deliver the Secret with External Secrets, sealed-secrets or a similar tool. The to block is only needed when MinIO runs in the cluster and you want to narrow the egress rule.

Notes for MinIO:

  • Create a MinIO user with a policy limited to the bucket and prefix, in the same shape as the IAM policy below. Do not use the root user.
  • Use https://. The chart refuses a plain http:// endpoint with env=production, and the api refuses it at boot unless SB_ENV=dev, including when the settings come from secrets.existingSecret.
  • region must match the region the server is configured with. MinIO uses us-east-1 unless you set another one.
  • sse: AES256 needs server-side encryption configured on the MinIO server (for example with MinIO KES). Without it, uploads that request SSE fail, so use sse: "" and let the server's own settings apply.

For local development, the api repository's docker-compose.yml runs a MinIO service and creates the bucket. See Running locally with docker compose.

docs.title: Least-privilege IAM policy
docs.text:
